## AI Agents for Business: When to Use One

An agent earns a place in the business only when the job branches and a person still checks the output. If the steps don't change, write the workflow and stop. Anthropic's December 2024 essay says to start with the simplest solution, and it separates a fixed workflow from an agent that directs its own tools.[^anthropic] We like that split because vendors have spent a year sanding it down. Everything is called an agent now, including a reminder that fires the same way every time. A reminder is a workflow. An agent is what you need when the next step depends on what the last step found, and you can't write every branch in advance. Even then, a person owns the stop. An agent without that person is a risk with a nickname.

The [people guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-people-low) is the matching fix when the gap is who checks, not which model you rent. The [definition](/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent) is the vocabulary, if the word itself has started to slide around the table. The [agentic comparison](/blog/ai-agents-vs-agentic-ai) is the next distinction, for when someone wants a fancier noun than the job deserves. Most owners we sit with don't need the fancier noun. They need one job held until a named person says it can leave.

## Eight jobs, each with a stop

Inbox triage waits for a person before anything is sent. Meeting notes wait before they become tasks. Quote follow-up waits before a price goes out. Invoice questions wait before a payment promise. Inventory exceptions wait before a purchase. Support replies wait before they reach the customer. Schedule changes wait before a customer is told. A weekly report waits before it is treated as the record.

Those eight are the only list we'd start from. Each one already happens in a shop, a clinic, or a trades desk. Each one has a moment where a wrong move is felt by a customer or by the books. The agent, if you use one, prepares. The person in the right-hand column decides. If you can't point at that person on a Tuesday, you don't have a candidate. You have a demo.

<!--image:2-->

| Job | What the person still does |
| --- | --- |
| Inbox triage | Decides what is actually sent |
| Meeting notes | Accepts the tasks |
| Quote follow-up | Approves the price |
| Invoice questions | Approves any promise to pay |
| Inventory exceptions | Approves the order |
| Support replies | Approves what the customer sees |
| Schedule changes | Approves the message |
| Weekly report | Accepts it as the record |

<!--cta:inline-->

Gartner said in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.[^gartner-agentic] The reasons are cost, unclear value, and inadequate risk controls. A job from the list above without a named checker is a candidate for that pile. Cost shows up when the agent keeps being allowed to look at more systems because nobody set the edge. Unclear value shows up when you can't say which wait in the list got shorter. Inadequate risk controls show up when the output doesn't wait. Cancellation isn't a moral. It's what happens to projects that were nouns before they were jobs. We'd rather you never start than join that pile with a good story about the pilot.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a clinic schedule as the case where an agent can be honest. This is a walkthrough. The front desk owns the book. The practitioner owns which visits are in scope. A patient asks to move a Tuesday visit to later in the week. Whether that works depends on what the book shows, on whether that practitioner does that kind of visit, and on a note billing will eventually need. You can't write every branch on a card. Someone has to look. An agent can look, draft the reply, and wait. The front desk still approves the message, because some patients need a call and some need two sentences, and the draft doesn't know the family. If the move changes the clinical plan, the practitioner approves it. That's the branch. The stop is a name, not a toggle labeled human in the loop that nobody's job description mentions.

Now take the shop's weekly report, which people love to call an agent because the word sounds busy. The report is the same shape every time. Yesterday's sales, the items that ran low, the invoices still open. Nothing in it depends on a discovery that rewrites the next step. A workflow can assemble it. A person accepts it as the record, or they don't and it stays a draft. Buying an agent for that assembly is how you pay for judgment you didn't need and skip the judgment you did. The acceptance is the whole point of the row in the table. If the bookkeeper doesn't accept the numbers, the report is a rumor that happens to be formatted.

A trades desk shows both shapes in one afternoon. Quote follow-up branches when the customer asks a question that changes the price path. The agent can gather the prior note and draft a reply. The owner approves the price before anything goes out. Invoice questions are stricter. A promise to pay is never the agent's to make. The person approves any promise. Inventory exceptions wait before a purchase, because ordering the wrong part is a truck roll. Support replies wait before the customer sees them. Schedule changes wait before a customer is told the van is coming. Meeting notes wait before they become tasks the lead tech didn't agree to. Inbox triage waits before anything is sent, including the cheerful draft that would have gone to the wrong thread. None of these require a new department. They require the wait to be real. A wait that is "usually someone glances" is not a wait. It's a wish.

## How we'd run it

First, write the job as if it were a plain workflow. Who starts it. What they produce. Who receives it. If you can finish that page without a branch, stop and ship the workflow. Anthropic's advice to start simpler is the whole method. The agent is the exception you earn, not the default you announce.

Second, circle the step where the next action depends on what you found. On the clinic book, the next message depends on the open slots and on whether the visit is in scope. On quote follow-up, the next sentence depends on whether the customer's question changed the job. If you can't circle a step like that, you circled a feeling. Feelings don't get a project.

Third, if you circled one, name the person who approves, using the table as the floor not the ceiling. Schedule changes: someone approves the message. Invoice questions: someone approves any promise to pay. Write the name of the human who works your desk, not the role "operations." If that person is "whoever is free," you have already described the cancellation. Free people don't check. Named people do, on their grouchiest morning.

Fourth, define the wrongness before you turn anything on. A moved visit on the wrong day. A price the owner never said. A payment promise the bookkeeper wouldn't make. A report treated as the books when it was still a draft. The risk control is that sentence plus a place where the output sits until the sentence is satisfied. Gartner's reasons aren't abstract here. Inadequate risk controls are a send button with no waiting room.

Fifth, run one job from the list and leave the others waiting on a person in the old way. Inbox triage or schedule changes are enough. Don't light up quote follow-up, support replies, and the weekly report in the same breath. One branch, one checker, one week of real messages. If the checker starts bypassing the wait because the draft is "usually fine," you learned something bad. Usually fine is how the wrong one leaves the building.

Sixth, revisit only after the first job is dull. Dull means the person still checks, the branch still matters, and you can say what value showed up without inventing a chart. If you can't, turn it off before cost becomes the reason someone else turns it off for you. Ending a small experiment is a success. Feeding it until the end of a hype cycle is how that canceled pile gets its next member.

## Common mistakes

Calling every automation an agent is the mistake the vocabulary notes exist to stop. A fixed sequence that files a photo and waits for a price is a workflow. It can be excellent. It doesn't get better because you rename it. We've watched owners pay an agent premium for a checklist, then feel cheated when the checklist behaved like a checklist. It was honest. The brochure wasn't.

Letting the output send itself is the mistake that reaches a customer. The table is blunt on purpose. Someone decides what is actually sent. Someone approves what the customer sees. Someone approves the message about a schedule change. Remove those sentences and you have a confident drafter with the keys. Confidence isn't authorization. The front desk's knowledge of who needs a phone call will not be in the prompt you wrote on a calm afternoon.

Starting from the model instead of the branch is how pilots get expensive and vague. Someone wants "an agent for the business" the way they might want a new hire with no seat. There is no seat called the business. There is inbox triage, or there isn't. There is a weekly report someone must accept, or there is a PDF that will be quoted as fact. Pick the row. If none of the rows hurt this month, you don't have an agent project. You have curiosity. Curiosity can read the definition post. It shouldn't sign a platform agreement.

Ignoring the cancellation forecast because it sounds like someone else's enterprise problem is how small firms get a smaller version of the same ending. Over 40% is not a large-company-only weather report. Cost, unclear value, and inadequate risk controls fit a clinic and a trades desk perfectly well. Your version won't make the newspaper. It will make a monthly bill and a queue of drafts nobody trusts. That's an adequate disaster. You don't need a bigger one to take the warning.

Staffing the check with a committee is the polite version of having no checker. "Someone will review" means the draft sits until it doesn't. Write one name. Give that person the authority to say no without a meeting. If the job is important enough for an agent, it's important enough for a name. If it isn't important enough for a name, it isn't important enough for an agent.

## What we'd do

We'd start with a workflow and make the agent earn the exception. That's the opinion, and we hold it when the demo is charming. Charming is not a branch. A branch is a schedule that changes what you're allowed to say, or a customer question that changes a price. If we can't see that on a real job from last week, we ship the fixed path and we go home. Home is a good outcome. Not every visit should end with a new system.

We'd put the person's name in the checkpoint before anything is turned on, and we'd use the table as a contract. The person decides what is sent, accepts the tasks, approves the price, approves any promise to pay, approves the order, approves what the customer sees, approves the message, and accepts the report as the record. If a proposal won't attach a name to the row you picked, the proposal is the risk control failure showing up early. Believe it.

We wouldn't run the whole list to feel modern. One job, held at the stop, beats eight half-starts that will be canceled for the reasons Gartner already gave. If you want a test this week, pick schedule changes or inbox triage, write the name of the approver, and refuse every extra system until that approver has lived with the wait. The agent can be added when the wait is real. It doesn't get to create the wait by existing.

## AI Agents vs Agentic AI: A Plain Split

An AI agent directs its own tools toward a goal, and agentic AI is the wider label for many of those systems across a company. The words get sold as if they were the same purchase. They are not.

An AI agent, in Anthropic's December 2024 essay, is a system that directs its own tools toward a goal.[^anthropic] A workflow is the opposite: the steps are written in advance. Agentic AI is the category vendors use when they mean many such systems, often across a company. The words are not interchangeable. We repeat that often because a deck will use the wider word for a single inbox rule, and the owner walks out thinking they bought a workforce.

The [definition](/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent) is the short version of the split between a path you wrote and a model that chooses. The [jobs list](/blog/ai-agents-for-business) is where one agent might actually sit. The [people guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-people-mid) is who has to check the output. If you cannot name that person, the rest of the vocabulary does not matter yet.

## What the forecast says

Gartner said in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.[^gartner-agentic] The reasons are cost, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls. Read those reasons as a checklist you can fail on purpose. A project with no named job will look unclear. A project nobody can halt will look like a risk problem. A project that needs three new tools and a consultant to explain them will look expensive, and then it will stop.

The same note said 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously by 2028, up from 0% in 2024, and that 33% of enterprise software will include agentic AI by 2028, up from less than 1% in 2024. Hold both forecasts at once. A lot of software will grow an agentic feature. A large share of the projects that chase the label will be canceled. The feature arriving in a product you already pay for is a different event from a program you launch because the word showed up in a board slide.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

If you can write the steps, you want a workflow. If the next step depends on what the last step found, you may want an agent, and you still want a person who can stop it. Calling that agentic does not change the checkpoint.

We use the forecast as a brake, not as a scare. Cancellation is what happens when the job was never specific enough to survive a budget meeting. It is also what happens when the risk control is a sentence in a policy nobody on the desk has read. You can avoid both without swearing off the tool. Name the decision. Name the checker. Keep the wider program on the shelf until that pair has worked on real afternoons.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Walk a small clinic with us. This is a scene, not a study, and it has no score attached. Nora owns the practice. One person runs the front desk. Dr. Patel sees patients. The phones pile up after lunch, mostly people who want to know whether a symptom can wait, whether a form was received, and whether tomorrow's visit is still on.

A workflow can carry the parts that do not change. A missed call becomes a task. The form either arrived or it did not. A reminder goes out the afternoon before, with the address and what to bring. The front desk lead already does this. Writing it down does not require a new category of software. It requires the front desk lead's order, and a screen that will not skip the "what to bring" line when the day gets rude.

An agent is the narrower ask. A patient writes that the rash spread and they also have a fever, and they want to know if they should come in today. The next step depends on what the note contains. A model could draft a reply that offers the urgent slot and tells them what to watch for, using only the phrases Dr. Patel has approved. The front desk lead still sends it. Dr. Patel still owns anything that sounds like a diagnosis. The agent picked a tool, the template and the schedule, inside bounds. That is one agent. It is not an agentic program.

Agentic AI, the way the word gets used on calls, would be the bigger bet. One system talks to the schedule, another drafts the chart note, another chases the referral, another updates the billing code, and they hand work to each other while Nora is with a patient. That is the shape of the projects in the cancellation forecast. Cost shows up as four subscriptions and a person whose job becomes watching them. Value stays unclear because nobody can say which decision got better. Risk control fails the first time a draft implies a diagnosis and leaves the building. We would not start there. We would start with the front desk lead's reminder path, then one draft on the fever note, with send still human.

The roles are the point of the walk-through. Nora decides which phrases are allowed. The front desk lead is the checker who can throw a draft away. Dr. Patel is the only person who closes a clinical question. A vendor who cannot point at those three seats, and who calls the whole bundle agentic because it sounds larger, is selling the category. They are not selling the checkpoint.

## How we'd run it

We would separate the words on a single page before anyone signs an order.

First, write the job as one decision. "Reply to a same-day symptom note with an approved phrase, or book the urgent slot, and never invent a diagnosis." If the job is "make the clinic agentic," throw it out and start again.

Second, list the steps the front desk lead already does that never change. Log the call, check the form, send the reminder, hold the chart for the clinician. That list is a workflow. Build it. Do not wait for a platform to discover it.

Third, circle the one place where the next step depends on what the message says. Symptom plus fever is a fork. A reminder is not. The fork is the only candidate for an agent. Everything else stays on the path you wrote.

Fourth, write the bounds in the front desk lead's language. Allowed tools: the approved phrases and the urgent column on the schedule. Forbidden: naming a condition, promising a medication, telling someone to stay home. If a phrase is not on the card, the draft does not use it.

Fifth, name the checker on the rota, not in a policy PDF. The front desk lead on the desk days. The backup coordinator when the front desk lead is out. Dr. Patel for anything the card does not cover. The stop condition is simple. Missing fever detail, an angry message, or a phrase that is not on the card, and the draft dies.

Sixth, run last week's real messages with the names removed. Nora and the front desk lead mark the drafts they would have refused. Fix the card until the refusals match their judgment. Only then let it draft against today's inbox. Calling the result agentic adds nothing. The checkpoint is the same either way.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is using the wide word for a narrow tool. A reminder sequence is a workflow. A chatbot that waits for a person to paste a question is one prompt. Neither becomes agentic because the proposal says so. The staff then expects a system of actors, and they get a mail merge.

The second mistake is starting with the constellation. Several tools, several handoffs, nobody who can draw the path on a whiteboard. That is the shape Gartner expects a large share of projects to abandon by the end of 2027, for cost, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls. A clinic does not need to donate itself to that share.

The third mistake is treating the 2028 lines as a deadline for your front desk. 15% of day-to-day work decisions made autonomously, and 33% of enterprise software including agentic AI, are statements about a market. They are not a due date for Nora. Software you already own may grow a feature. You still choose whether the front desk lead is allowed to rely on it.

The fourth mistake is a checker who exists only on paper. "The clinical lead reviews outputs" means nothing on a Tuesday when the lead is in a room and the draft is in the outbox. If the person who can stop it is not at the desk, you do not have the control. You have a sentence.

The fifth mistake is letting a draft sound like Dr. Patel. Patients do not hear "language model." They hear the clinic. A warm sentence that implies a diagnosis is a clinical act. Keep it off the card, and kill the draft that sneaks one in.

The sixth mistake is buying because 0% feels embarrassing. The note said autonomous day-to-day decisions sat at 0% in 2024. That is a baseline, not an insult. Moving off it without a named decision is how the cancellation reasons show up in a smaller budget.

## What we'd do

We would buy the workflow first and the single agent second, and we would leave the agentic program unsold. Our opinion is that the wider word is doing sales work. It makes a reminder bot sound like a strategy, and it makes a careful one-agent pilot sound small. Small is the correct size until the front desk lead can refuse a draft without calling a vendor.

If the next step truly depends on what the note found, one agent, one card of phrases, one person who can stop it. If the steps are already writable, stay with the workflow and spend the money on the afternoon the front desk lead is underwater. The June 2025 forecast is not a reason to hide from the tool. It is a reason to refuse a project that cannot name its checker. We would rather be the clinic that canceled nothing, because we never started the project that deserved canceling.

## AI Automation Agency vs Consultant: Who to Hire

Hire a consultant to name the job, and hire an agency only after that naming is done. An AI consultant names the job, the data, and the stop. An automation agency builds the system after that naming is done. Hiring the agency first produces a build with no owner. We've watched that sequence in the wrong order more than once. The proposal arrives with staff, a toolset, and a start date. Nobody in the room can say which output a person still has to check. The build proceeds anyway, because the calendar was the only decision anyone made.

The [consultant note](/blog/ai-consultant-for-small-business) is the question list we wish owners had in their pocket before the first sales call. The [buy-or-build note](/blog/off-the-shelf-ai-or-custom-software) is whether to build at all. The [decision guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-decision-mid) is the matching score when the choice itself is the thing you're avoiding. Hiring is a decision. Score it before you sign. A signature on a vague scope is not a strategy. It's a hope with a payment schedule.

## Two training figures, two populations

Microsoft's 2024 index says only 25% of companies were planning to offer generative AI training.[^microsoft] Statistics Canada's 2025 report says 38.9% of Canadian businesses that already use AI had trained staff.[^statcan] Those are different populations. One is a plan among companies. The other is training among businesses that already use AI. Do not average them. A pitch that slides the two numbers into "about a third of firms train people" has invented a fact. The plan figure is about companies that were intending to offer training. The Canadian figure is about businesses already using AI that had actually trained staff. Intending and having done it are different. Companies and AI-using businesses are different. Countries and survey windows are different. If a consultant or an agency treats them as one knob, they are not reading. They are decorating.

<!--image:2-->

McKinsey's 2025 survey says 23% are scaling an agentic system somewhere, and 39% are experimenting.[^mckinsey] An agency pitch that quotes only a use figure is selling the experiment. Experimenting is the larger group. Scaling somewhere is the smaller one, and "somewhere" matters. Somewhere is not "in the job you care about," and it is not "in a firm the size of yours." We say this because the word agent shows up in proposals before anyone has admitted they are still in the experiment. An experiment can be the right buy if it is labeled as one, with a stop and a person. An experiment sold as a finished operation is how the owner ends up maintaining a demo.

<!--cta:inline-->

Pay a consultant to refuse the work that a product already does. Pay an agency when the process is written and the checker is named. The refusal is the valuable part, and it's the part a build contract is bad at. A builder is paid to build. A namer can be paid to say "don't." If you only hire people who are paid when the project starts, you will get a project. You may not get a job worth doing.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a clinic that almost hired an agency to "put an agent on the front desk." This is a walkthrough, not a scoreboard. The owner had three calls in a week and a folder of proposals. The front desk still books by phone and by a form on the site. The practitioner still decides which visits are in scope. Billing still waits for a note that the visit happened. Ask what the agent would be allowed to send and the room goes quiet. Ask what happens when the draft is wrong and the room gets quieter. That quiet is the consultant's whole engagement. Name the job. Name the data the job is allowed to see. Name the stop.

In that room we'd send them to a consultant before any build. The consultant's output is a page, not a login. The page might say: the front desk drafts reminders, a person sends them, the practitioner is the stop when the reminder includes a clinical instruction, and billing is not in this job at all. It might also say the booking product they already pay for sends a plain reminder, so don't build one. That refusal is worth more than a sprint. An agency that starts before the page exists will build the reminder anyway, because a reminder is easy to demo. Easy to demo is not the same as missing.

A trades desk is the other shape, and it's where an agency can be the right call. The quote steps are already written. The office manager logs the address. The lead tech files measurements before leaving the driveway. The owner prices, and the price is the stop. The bookkeeper doesn't open an invoice until the yes is written down. A product they tried doesn't hold site photos and supplier notes in one place. The checker has a name. That's a build. Even then we'd want the agency to repeat the stop back to us before they estimate. If they talk about agents and never say the owner's name next to the price, they're selling the experiment McKinsey's larger share is still in.

A shop is usually neither a big consulting saga nor a custom build. The owner wants someone to "do AI" because a neighbor did. The clerk already knows the reorder. The bookkeeper already has a late-invoice list. A consultant who earns the fee will point at one of those, refuse the rest, and go home. An agency that earns the fee will only show up if that one job truly needs a system no product covers. Most weeks, it doesn't. Paying either of them to rediscover the clerk's list is a polite way to avoid deciding.

## How we'd run it

First, write the job in one sentence a new hire could read. Not "AI for the front desk." The front desk sends appointment reminders after a person reads them. If you can't get to a sentence like that, you are hiring a mood. Moods are expensive when they come with a team.

Second, write the data the job may touch and the data it may not. Reminders can see the time and the place. They can't see the clinical note unless a named practitioner says so. Quotes can see the site measurements. They can't invent a price. If the data line is "whatever the model needs," you don't have a boundary. You have a hope that the vendor will be careful. Vendors are careful about their scope. You have to be careful about yours.

Third, name the checker in the same sentence as the job. A person, a place where the output waits, and what happens if it's wrong. A checkpoint nobody owns is not a checkpoint. We'd rather delay the hire than sign a scope where "someone will review" is the only human. Someone is not a name. Everyone goes home.

Fourth, ask whether a product already does this. The consultant is paid to refuse that work. If the booking tool already sends the plain reminder, stop. If the books already flag the late invoice, stop. Bring an agency in only for the gap that remains after that refusal. The buy-or-build note is the longer version of this step. Don't skip it because an agency proposal is already pretty.

Fifth, separate the training story from the build story. The 25% figure is companies planning to offer training. The 38.9% figure is AI-using businesses that had trained staff. Neither figure is a promise that your clerk will be shown the path. Put the showing in the scope. A launch without a person who can run the job next Tuesday is a launch into the owner's memory, which is where the work already lived.

Sixth, if the proposal mentions agents, ask whether they are scaling or experimenting, and make them say which. 23% and 39% are not invitations. They're a warning about language. If the honest answer is experiment, write "experiment" at the top of the scope, with a date you'll decide to keep it or turn it off. If they can't say, you're buying a word.

## Common mistakes

Hiring the agency because the proposal had more pages is the mistake with the nicest stationery. Pages are not a named job. A bench of people is not a checker. We've sat with owners who chose the thicker folder because it felt like seriousness. Seriousness is a person who will tell you not to start. The thinner conversation is often the one that saves the quarter. We don't mean a cheap conversation. We mean a conversation that is allowed to end in no.

Averaging the training figures is the mistake that makes everyone sound informed. Someone says firms don't train, and someone else quotes the other survey as if it were the same study, and the room nods. They aren't. One is a plan in a 2024 index of companies. One is training already done among Canadian businesses that use AI, in a 2025 report. Use either number alone, with its population, or use neither. The fake average will be repeated to your staff as if it were a law. It isn't.

Buying the experiment under a scaling headline is how agent language gets into a clinic that needed a reminder. McKinsey's split is the antidote if you actually say it out loud in the meeting. Most of the respondents in that survey were not scaling. If your seller only quotes a use number, ask what happened to the people who were still experimenting. Then ask which group the proposal belongs to. Silence is an answer. Treat it as one.

Leaving the refusal out of the contract is how you pay twice. You pay the agency to build the thing the product already did, and you pay the product to keep doing it. A consultant who won't refuse is a salesperson with a notebook. We'd rather pay for a no on a single page than pay for a yes that duplicates the booking tool. Put the right to stop in writing before the build has a channel and a standup.

Skipping the owner of the output is the last one, and it survives all the others. The scope names a platform. It doesn't name the office manager. On the first real day the draft is ready and nobody's job includes looking at it. The agency did what it was paid to do. The consultant, if you had one, either wasn't listened to or wasn't asked. The draft waits in a queue that is technically a success. Customers never see a success. They see whatever escaped.

## What we'd do

We'd hire the namer first, almost every time, and we'd pay them to be willing to end the engagement with a refusal. That's the opinion. A clinic that can't say what the front desk is allowed to send doesn't need an agency yet. A shop whose late invoices already live in the bookkeeping product doesn't need either of them. A trades desk with the steps written, the price owned by a named person, and a gap no product covers is the rare room where we'd call a builder. Even there, the builder doesn't get to rename the job.

We wouldn't let a single training statistic into the proposal without its population sitting next to it. We wouldn't let "agent" into the scope unless someone can show the step that branches and the person who stops it. We wouldn't sign a start date that arrives before the page. Dates are easy. Pages are the work. If the seller needs the date to hold their staff together, that is their problem to solve after you know what you're buying.

If you only do one thing before the next call, write the sentence with the job and the checker, and ask the seller to repeat it without adding a platform. If they can't, you are not late. You are early, which is the correct time to be early. The experiment will still be there next month. Your name on a vague scope is harder to get back.

## AI Automation for Small Business: Which Job First

AI automation for a small business is a choice of which job goes first, not a catalog of tools. We score a candidate on four things, in words. How often the job happens. How stable the rules are. Whether a system can read the data. What a wrong answer costs. High volume, stable rules, readable data, and a cheap catch belong first. A rare decision with an expensive mistake does not, no matter how glamorous the demo made it look.

The [pressure guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/pressure) is where we ask the work to show its slow spot. The [mapping note](/blog/business-process-automation-ai) is the step before a tool, when the job is still a story in someone's head. The [agency note](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) is the hiring question that comes after you know the job and not before. If you hire first, you will be sold a stack. The stack is not the decision.

Owners tell us they want "automation" the way a person wants a cleaner garage. They want the feeling of less mess. The feeling arrives, if it arrives, after one ugly repeated job gets a written path. It does not arrive because a menu of features was long.

## What the surveys already count

Statistics Canada, for the second quarter of 2025, found that 12.2% of businesses used AI to produce goods or deliver services, up from 6.1% a year earlier.[^statcan] Among businesses that used AI, text analytics accounted for 35.7% and marketing automation for 23.1%. 40.1% had developed new workflows, and 38.9% had trained staff. Read that as a queue, not as a ranking of your character. Sorting text shows up. Marketing that can be counted shows up. New workflows and trained people show up beside the tool, which is the part vendors mention last.

<!--image:2-->

The Chamber's 2025 report says 58% of small businesses use generative AI, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023.[^chamber] That is a different question. Opening a generative tool is not the same as putting AI inside delivery. A shop can live inside the Chamber figure and outside the Statistics Canada figure on the same afternoon. If a seller quotes only the larger share, ask them to say the smaller one too. The smaller one is closer to the job you are about to change.

<!--cta:inline-->

Read the StatCan list as the practical queue: sort text, run marketing that can be measured, write a workflow that did not exist, and train the people who will run it. Run the four-part test on each one before you buy anything. A job that fails the test can still be done by a person. That is not a defeat. That is the test working.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Come behind the counter of a small distributor that sells parts to repair shops. Walk-through only. We are not claiming a measured outcome. The owner still knows the odd customers by voice. A bookkeeper posts invoices three mornings a week. A floor lead pulls orders. Someone, often the owner's niece, is "in charge of social" in the sense that she feels guilty about it.

Three piles sit on the desk, and only one of them deserves a machine.

The invoice pile is boring and constant. Vendors send scans. The lines repeat. The rules are dull and mostly stable: match the vendor, match the amount, flag a duplicate, do not invent a category the bookkeeper has not approved. The data can be read if the scan is decent, and when it cannot, a person still has the paper. A wrong suggestion costs a correction before anything is posted, as long as the bookkeeper is the one who posts. This pile passes the test. It is the job we would touch first.

The social pile looks easier and is a worse first job than people think. The niece can already draft a caption with a generative tool. That is the Chamber kind of use, and it is fine. Marketing automation, in the Statistics Canada sense among businesses already using AI, is a real category. It still fails our test if nobody knows what a good post is for, or if the product names change every week because the floor lead hears them wrong. Volume is low. Rules are mushy. A wrong caption is usually cheap, which is the only part of the test it passes. Cheap is not enough when the other parts wobble. Leave it as a human draft.

The third pile is a furious one-off. A repair shop claims a part failed and wants a credit, a lecture, and a promise. The rules are not stable because the relationship is the rule. The data is a phone call plus a photo plus ten years of memory in the owner's head. A wrong reply costs the account. This job fails on purpose. We would not automate the apology. We would let the owner make it, and we would keep the tool away from the thread so it cannot sound smooth and be wrong.

Put the bookkeeper in charge of the invoice experiment, not the niece and not the owner. She knows a duplicate when she sees one. The floor lead's role is to say when a vendor name on the scan is the nickname they use in the warehouse, not the legal name. The owner's role is to refuse to add the angry-customer job "while we are at it." That refusal is the whole strategy.

## How we'd run it

We run the choice as a filter. Anything that survives is allowed to become a small install. Anything that does not survive stays manual without shame.

First, we list the candidate jobs in the owner's words, on one page, without tool names. Invoices. Captions. The angry credit. Maybe a mailbox full of "do you have this part" questions. We ask which one happens even when everyone is tired. The tired job is usually the right one. Heroic rare jobs attract software and then starve.

Second, we score each candidate on the four tests, out loud, with the person who does the work. How often. How stable the rules are. Can a system read the source, or is the source a memory. What does a wrong answer cost, and can a named person catch it before it leaves. The invoice passes. The caption is a maybe that we park. The credit fails. We write the fails down so they do not creep back into the proposal as "phase two."

Third, we map the passing job before we look at products. That map is the point of the [mapping note](/blog/business-process-automation-ai). Who touches the scan. Where it is saved. What the bookkeeper changes by hand. What she refuses to let a suggestion decide. If we cannot draw that with her, we are not ready to buy. The [pressure guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/pressure) is useful here when the owner insists every job is equally slow. It is not. One of them is eating the morning.

Fourth, we pick a tool only after the map exists, and we prefer the dull one that fits the map. A scanner-and-suggest flow the bookkeeper can reject is enough. We do not add a customer-facing bot because the invoice project feels too plain to brag about. Plain is the point. If the owner wants help choosing who should build or advise, that conversation waits until now, and it belongs on the [agency note](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant), not at the start.

Fifth, we train the person who will run it, and we count the project as unfinished until she has. Statistics Canada found that, among businesses that used AI, 38.9% had trained staff and 40.1% had developed new workflows. Those are not decorations next to the 12.2% who used AI in production. They are the reason production use is still the smaller fact. We would rather delay the switch-on than hand the bookkeeper a login and a wish.

## Common mistakes

Starting from a tool menu is the mistake the catalogs encourage. The menu has marketing, chat, invoices, and a promise that they share a brain. Your desk does not share a brain. The invoice rules are stable. The angry customer is not. Buying the bundle because it is bundled imports a failing job into a passing one.

Treating generative use as automation is the Chamber trap. 58% of small businesses in the 2025 report use generative AI, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. The niece drafting a caption may already be in that crowd. She has not automated delivery. If you report her habit to yourself as "we automated marketing," you will skip the bookkeeper, who was the actual opportunity.

Automating the rare, expensive decision because it is painful is the emotional mistake. Pain is not a test. The credit argument hurts, so the owner wants it gone. Gone, in software, means a smooth reply that might be false. The catch is not cheap. Leave it.

Forgetting training because the interface looks friendly is how the new workflow dies. A friendly screen still has a reject button nobody was taught to trust. 38.9% of the businesses already using AI had trained staff. That is not a high bar and many still miss it. We would miss it too if we let the launch meeting be a tour of buttons.

Copying another firm's first job is the last one. Their text sort might be sacred and yours might be a mess of photos. Their marketing might be a weekly rhythm and yours might be guilt. The surveys describe crowds. The four tests describe your morning. Use the crowd to get ideas. Use the morning to decide.

## What we'd do

We would put the invoice, or whatever your version of the repeated readable pile is, in front of every shinier idea. That is the opinion. Text analytics accounted for 35.7% of the uses among businesses that used AI in the Statistics Canada count, and marketing automation for 23.1%. Both are legitimate. We still start where a wrong line can be caught by the bookkeeper before money moves. Marketing drafts can wait in the niece's hands, edited by a person, until the rules are boring enough to write down.

We would not let the Chamber's 58% set the pace. That figure, and the climb from 23% in 2023 through 40% in 2024, says generative tools spread. It does not say your delivery should be handed to one. The production figure, 12.2% in the second quarter of 2025, up from 6.1% a year earlier, is the stricter crowd. Join it on one job, with a new workflow and a trained person, or do not claim you joined it.

If you are unsure which pile is eating the week, open the [pressure guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/pressure) and make the slow job confess. Then map it, using the [mapping note](/blog/business-process-automation-ai), before you talk to a builder. When you do need a person, the [agency note](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) will keep you from hiring a platform when you needed a checker. We would rather automate one dull pile well than announce that you "run on automation" while the bookkeeper still retypes every scan.

## AI Consultant for Small Business: What to Ask

A useful AI consultant for a small business can name the job, the data, and the person who is allowed to stop the work. If an off-the-shelf product already does that job, the honest advice is to buy the product and skip the custom project. We would rather lose the engagement than invent a build to justify a fee. That is how the [studio](/) works. The hiring split, consultant versus a firm that wants to own the install, is the [agency comparison](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant). What happens when a pretty proof never becomes a process is the [stall note](/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall).

Bring the person who does the job into the first meeting. An owner alone will be sold a platform. The office manager, the bookkeeper, or the dispatcher will ask where the file lives, and that question is worth more than the slide with the architecture. If the consultant looks annoyed by it, you have learned something cheap.

We are opinionated about this because we have watched the alternative. A pitch that starts with a tool name has skipped the work. You can always get back to a tool. You cannot easily get back the month you spent implementing the wrong promise.

## What gets canceled

Gartner said in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing cost, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls.[^gartner-agentic] In a poll of 3,412 respondents, 19% said their organization had made significant investments in agentic AI, 42% had made conservative investments, 8% had made none, and 31% were waiting or unsure. Gartner also said only about 130 vendors offered what it considered real agentic products. Sit with that last line before you let a proposal use the word agent as decoration. The label is common. The thing Gartner was willing to call real was not.

<!--image:2-->

McKinsey's 2025 survey puts the same gap in different numbers. 88% report regular AI use in at least one function, up from 78% a year earlier.[^mckinsey] 23% are scaling an agentic system somewhere, and 39% are experimenting. A consultant who quotes only the first figure is describing use, not a finished system. Ask them to say the second pair of figures without flinching. If they cannot, they are selling the feeling of being current.

<!--cta:inline-->

Red flags are specific. Guaranteed rankings ignore Google's guide, which says generative features are still SEO.[^google] Nobody can guarantee a ranking in an overview, and a person who does is telling you they will also bluff the rest of the engagement. No data plan means the source of truth was never named. No handover means the business cannot run the thing after the invoice. We treat those three as reasons to end the meeting, not as issues to "workshop."

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Sit in on a hiring conversation at a small clinic. Again, this is a walk-through we use, not a scoreboard. The owner-dentist wants help. The office manager, who actually runs recall and the front desk, is in the room because we asked her to be. The bookkeeper is not there yet. She will matter when the invoice arrives, and she should see the proposal before anyone signs.

The first consultant opens a laptop and names a platform. He talks about agents that will "handle the patient journey." He has not asked where the appointment book lives. He has not asked about the paper list of people who do not want texts. When the office manager asks who checks a message before it goes out, he says the system has guardrails. Guardrails are not a name. She writes nothing down. That is the right instinct.

The second consultant does not open a tool. She asks the office manager to describe last Monday, including the part that went wrong. The wrong part was a reminder that went to a patient who was already in the chair for treatment, because the recall list and the treatment list do not share a brain. The consultant writes a sentence: draft cleaning reminders from the appointment record only, and the office manager sends them. She asks where the do-not-contact names live. She asks what the manager should do when she is out. She says, out loud, that if a shelf product already drafts that reminder inside the practice software, they should buy that and stop talking to her.

We would hire the second person, and we would still make her put the stop rule in the proposal. Keep going only if the manager can clear the queue in the time they hold on the calendar. Stop if the drafts keep choosing the wrong patients. A consultant who will not write the stop is planning to linger. Lingering is how a small fee becomes the kind of project Gartner expects a large share of agentic work to cancel.

Notice who did the real interview. It was the office manager, not the owner. The owner felt the pain. The manager knows the drawer with the paper list. A good consultant will talk to the owner about money and risk, and will talk to the manager about the Monday. A weak one will charm the owner and avoid the manager, because the manager asks questions that shrink the proposal. Let the proposal shrink. A smaller true job is a better buy than a large foggy one.

## How we'd run it

We run a hiring conversation as a filter. The consultant is not owed a second meeting.

First, we send the questions ahead, in writing, so nobody can claim they were ambushed. What job will change. Where does the data live. Who checks the output, by name. How will we know it failed. What will you refuse to build. If the reply is a calendar link and a deck, and none of those answers, we do not take the meeting. Politeness is not a reason to donate an hour.

Second, we hold the meeting with the person who does the work, not only the owner. We ask the consultant to restate the job in one sentence the staff can repeat. If the sentence contains a tool name and no verb the staff recognize, we send them back. "Implement the platform" is not a job. "Draft the cleaning reminder and wait" is a job.

Third, we ask the buy-versus-build question directly, and we watch the face. If an off-the-shelf product already does this, will you say so. The honest answer is yes, and then a short list of what they would still help with, such as the wording and the checker. The dishonest answer is a custom build that recreates a feature the practice software already sells. We have no patience for that recreation. It flatters the consultant's hours and leaves the manager with two systems.

Fourth, we demand a handover before we talk about price. Who can run this when you leave. Where the rejects are written. What the bookkeeper will see on the invoice, in words, not only in a total. A price with no handover is a subscription to a person. That can be fine for advice. It is a bad way to buy a system. The [agency comparison](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) is the page we use when the owner is confused about which kind of help they even want.

Fifth, we check the red flags in the proposal language itself. Any promise of guaranteed rankings gets a no, because Google's own guide says generative features still depend on ordinary SEO. Any slide that quotes use without the scaling gap gets a question. Any plan that cannot name a risk control gets a no, which is the same reason Gartner gave for cancellation: cost, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls. We would rather be known as difficult in the first meeting than stuck in the project that gets canceled after the staff have already changed their week around it.

## Common mistakes

Hiring the best talker is the ordinary mistake, and it is human. The owner is busy and a clear voice feels like competence. Competence, in this work, sounds slower. It sounds like questions about a drawer full of paper. If you leave a meeting energized and unable to repeat the job sentence, you were entertained.

Leaving the operator out of the room is the structural mistake. The office manager will inherit the queue. If she meets the system on launch day, she will route around it, and she will be right. Invite her while the proposal can still change. If the consultant objects, that objection is the finding.

Accepting "agent" as a product category is how the poll gets ignored. In that Gartner poll of 3,412 respondents, 19% had made significant investments in agentic AI, 42% conservative investments, 8% none, and 31% were waiting or unsure. Only about 130 vendors met Gartner's bar for a real agentic product. A proposal that calls a reminder draft an agent is borrowing a word. Ask what the software does on a Monday. If the answer is "it drafts and a person sends," call it a draft. The plainer word will get you a plainer price.

Skipping the search-and-ranking fantasy is a mistake in the other direction too, when the consultant brings it unasked. Guaranteed placement in an AI overview is a red flag even if you never asked for marketing help. It tells you the rest of the claims are flexible. Google's guide is public. A person selling certainty against a public guide will sell certainty against your files as well.

Signing because the quote is small is the last trap. A small quote with no stop rule becomes a long quote. Cost is one of the reasons those projects get canceled. Get the stop in writing while the number still feels harmless.

## What we'd do

We would tell a lot of owners to buy the shelf product and send the consultant home. That is the opinion that loses us work, and we still hold it. Custom work is justified when the job is specific to your files and a product will not touch them, or when the value is the thinking and the handover rather than the code. It is not justified because a platform demo was impressive and the office manager was not in the room to object.

We would also quote the awkward survey figures in the proposal review, on purpose. Over 40% of agentic AI projects canceled by the end of 2027 is not a reason to avoid all help. It is a reason to demand a value you can point at and a risk control with a name. The McKinsey gap belongs in the same conversation. 88% using AI in at least one function, up from 78% a year earlier, will be in the consultant's mouth. 23% scaling an agentic system, and 39% experimenting, should be in yours. If they only brought the first number, they are describing a hobby and pricing it like a system.

If the proposal mentions search, rankings, or "being the answer" in a generative result, we stop and open Google's guide with them.[^google] Generative features are still SEO. Nobody serious guarantees the outcome. And if the proof they show you cannot survive a normal week, read the [stall note](/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall) before you fund a sequel. The [studio](/) will say buy the product when that is the truth. We think you should require the same sentence from anyone else you pay.

## AI for Small Business: What the Surveys Still Say

The useful question for a small business is which job actually changes. Two surveys from 2025 are still the clean public counts, and they do not measure the same thing. One asks whether a small business uses generative AI. The other asks whether a business used AI to produce the goods or deliver the service. You can say yes to the first and no to the second and be honest both times. Averaging them into a single "how behind are we" number is how owners buy the wrong project.

We wrote the full split in the [help note](/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses). What to do with the gap is the [strategy note](/blog/ai-strategy-for-small-business). How to score one firm, instead of scoring a country, is the [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment). A survey is a crowd. Your shop is one set of hands, one set of files, and one job that is slow this week. Start there.

We get asked which percentage to believe. We do not believe either one as a verdict on a single owner. We believe the wording of the question. If you skip the wording, you will spend a season chasing a rank that was never about your counter.

## Two questions, two answers

The Chamber's 2025 report says 58% of small businesses use generative AI, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023.[^chamber] That question is about use of a generative tool. Writing a product blurb, drafting a reply, sketching a social post, asking for a checklist. It counts the owner who opened the tool on a Tuesday and got something usable enough to edit. It does not ask whether the goods on the shelf were produced by a model, or whether the service the customer paid for was delivered by one.

<!--image:2-->

Statistics Canada, for 2025, found 12.2% of businesses used AI to produce goods or deliver services, up from 6.1% a year earlier.[^statcan] That is a harder, narrower question. It is about the thing you sell. A bakery that uses a tool to write the weekly email can sit inside the Chamber figure and outside the Statistics Canada figure. A shop that lets a model propose purchase orders, which a person then places, is edging toward the second question and still may not meet it. Read the verb. Produce. Deliver. Not draft. Not brainstorm. Not "we tried it."

<!--cta:inline-->

A firm can say yes to the Chamber question and no to the Statistics Canada question. Plan from the job you can name. Do not average the two percentages into a single readiness rate. This site does not publish an aggregate score from the Readiness Check. If someone offers you a blended "small business AI adoption" figure made from these two, they have glued different questions together and called the glue insight.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Walk a home-goods shop with us. This is an example, not a study, and we are not attaching a score to it. The owner buys from a few makers and from one wholesaler. A floor lead works the counter and knows which lamp has a chip in the glaze. A bookkeeper comes in part of the week and hates surprises in the inbox. There is no IT person. There is a group text.

Last winter the owner started using a generative tool for product descriptions. She pastes a few notes from the maker, asks for a short paragraph in her voice, and edits out anything that sounds like a catalog from nowhere. The floor lead does the same for a social caption when a new table arrives, then deletes the line that claims the wood is oak when it is not. That is real use. On the Chamber question, this shop says yes. Generative AI is in the week.

Nothing about that use produces the lamp or delivers the sale. The owner still chooses the maker. The floor lead still wraps the lamp, still tells the truth about the chip, still calls the customer when the freight is late. The bookkeeper still matches the invoice to the packing slip with her eyes. On the Statistics Canada question, this shop says no. AI is not producing the goods and it is not delivering the service. Both answers are correct. A consultant who collapses them into "you are an AI business now" or "you are behind the market" has not listened.

Here is the job that might move them toward the second question, if they ever want that. The wholesaler's invoices arrive as scans with line items the bookkeeper retypes. A tool that reads the scan and proposes the lines, with the bookkeeper still posting them, is closer to delivery of the back-office service than a prettier lamp description is. It is still not the shop "running on AI." It is one job, with a checker, touching the thing they already do to get paid. We would talk about that job for an hour before we ever mentioned the Chamber share.

The trap in this shop is pride in the wrong direction. The owner feels modern because the descriptions improved, and a nephew told her that most small businesses are already doing this. He was waving at the Chamber figure without saying the question. She also feels secretly behind because a podcast said only a small slice of firms use AI in production. That podcast was waving at a figure like the Statistics Canada one, again without the question. She is neither a laggard nor finished. She has a drafting habit and an untouched invoice pile.

## How we'd run it

We do not start by asking an owner where they rank. We start by forcing the two questions apart, then we pick a job.

First, we ask what they already open in a week. The shop owner will say the writing tool. We write that down as generative use, in the Chamber sense, and we do not praise it as a strategy. We also do not scold it. A decent product description that a human edits is a fair use of an afternoon. It is just not the same fact as AI inside delivery.

Second, we ask what the customer actually pays for, and what has to be true for the money to be earned. In the shop, that is the right object, in the condition the floor lead described, handed over or shipped, with the books able to explain the invoice. We look for any step in that chain where a model already acts. Usually there is none. We say so. The Statistics Canada question stays a no, and the no is useful. It stops the owner from advertising a capability she does not have.

Third, we pick one candidate job that could change the chain, and we describe it in a sentence a new hire could follow. For this shop we like the scanned invoice, not the caption. The sentence is: read the wholesaler scan, propose the lines, and wait for the bookkeeper to post. If the owner wants the caption "automated" instead, we will do it only after she admits it does not change delivery. Sometimes that is still worth a small habit. It is not worth a project with a name.

Fourth, we name the checker and the failure. The bookkeeper is the checker. Failure is a line that does not match the packing slip, or a vendor she does not recognize. If she cannot see the original scan beside the proposal, the job is not safe, and we do not turn it on. This is the same discipline as any other install. The survey cannot do it for her.

Fifth, we refuse the blended score. We will not tell this owner she is at some midpoint between the Chamber's use figure and Statistics Canada's production figure. Those populations and those verbs are different. The [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) scores her files, her people, and her job. The [strategy note](/blog/ai-strategy-for-small-business) is where the one-page plan goes after the job is chosen. The [help note](/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses) is the longer version of the split if a partner still wants to argue from a headline.

## Common mistakes

Quoting a single percentage in a staff meeting is the fastest way to start a useless argument. "Most small businesses already use it" points at the Chamber's 58% in the 2025 report, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. Someone on the floor hears that they are late. They are not late at wrapping lamps. They are being compared on a question about generative tools. Say the question or do not say the number.

The mirror mistake is shame from the smaller figure. 12.2% of businesses in the Statistics Canada count used AI to produce goods or deliver services in 2025, up from 6.1% a year earlier. An owner hears "almost nobody is really doing this" and either freezes or decides the whole topic is hype. Neither reaction picks a job. The smaller figure is a description of a strict question. It is not a personality test.

Averaging the two rates is the mistake we will interrupt out loud. A midpoint is not a readiness rate. The firms, the countries, and the verbs differ. This site does not publish an aggregate score from the Readiness Check, and we do not want a homemade one built in a spreadsheet either. If you need a number for your own business, it has to be about your business. A national blend cannot tell the bookkeeper whether the scan is readable.

Buying a tool to close the emotional gap is the costly version. The owner feels the distance between "we write blurbs" and "AI runs the shop," so she purchases something that promises to run the shop. Nothing in either survey asked her to do that. The surveys did not name her wholesaler, her chip in the glaze, or her bookkeeper's part-time days. A purchase that ignores those facts will stall for the ordinary reasons, and then the survey gets blamed.

Treating a yes on the Chamber question as a marketing claim is how trust frays. "We use AI" on the window, when what you use is a draft of a caption, invites a customer to expect something you do not do. We would rather the shop say nothing. The floor lead's honesty about the glaze is worth more than a badge.

## What we'd do

We would plan from the job, and we would say the Statistics Canada question out loud before we said the Chamber one. That is a preference, not a law. Drafting help is legitimate. It is also the easier yes, and it flatters the owner. The question about producing goods or delivering services is the one that changes payroll, mistakes, and what the customer receives. If the owner only has appetite for the draft, we will help her keep it human-edited and small. We will not call it an operating shift.

We would not tell the home-goods owner she is behind the 58%, and we would not tell her she has "arrived" because she might be inside it. Arrival is a job you can name on a slow Tuesday, with a checker who is a person. The move from 23% in 2023 to 40% in 2024 to 58% in the Chamber's 2025 report shows generative use spreading. The move from 6.1% to 12.2% in the Statistics Canada figures for 2025 shows a stricter behavior spreading more quietly. Both can be true. Your shop does not have to impersonate either crowd.

If a partner brings you a chart this week, ask which question was on the survey. If they cannot answer, put the chart down and open the [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment). If they can answer, and the question is about use rather than delivery, read the [help note](/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses) before you spend. When you are ready to choose the job on purpose, the [strategy note](/blog/ai-strategy-for-small-business) is the page we would write with you. We would rather be dull and specific than armed with a percentage that describes someone else's verb.

## An AI Implementation Framework in Five Stages

An AI implementation framework is the order of work you follow once the job is already named. NIST calls the risk side of that work Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.[^nist] We use five stages in plain words, because that is how the conversation actually goes when we sit with an owner. Name the job. Score the data. Write the process. Assign a checker. Then keep the work or stop it.

Most small firms we meet are still in the [Forming band](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/band/forming) while those stages are unfinished. A tool is open on someone's laptop. The rest is a hope. Hope is not a stage. If you skip one, you get the stall we describe in the [stall note](/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall). The score that should come before any build is the [readiness framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework). This note is only the order of work after that score exists.

We like a boring order. Owners like a demo. The demo feels like progress because someone in the room relaxes. The order feels like delay because it is a list. The list is the work. A framework that cannot be walked on a single page is a brochure, and we will not pretend a brochure runs on Monday.

## What the numbers say about the middle

McKinsey's 2025 survey says 88% report regular AI use in at least one function.[^mckinsey] That is the easy number, and it is the one a vendor will quote before the coffee arrives. The harder numbers sit beside it. 23% are scaling an agentic system somewhere, and 39% are experimenting. 29% of firms under $100 million are scaling, against nearly half of firms over $5 billion. No more than 10% scale agents in any one function.

Read that last line slowly if you run a shop, a clinic, or a trades desk. Regular use is a person opening a tool. Scaling inside one function means the function runs on a written process, with a person who can stop it. The gap between those two is where projects live as a browser tab nobody closes. We do not think a small firm is behind because it is not among the firms scaling an agentic system. We think it is on time if it can finish one function without lying about who checks the output.

<!--image:2-->

Cisco's 2025 survey of 8,000 leaders found pacesetters, near 13% of that sample, were 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production.[^cisco] Those leaders work in organizations with more than 500 employees. A small business can still copy the sequence those pacesetters used. Write the process, then put it into production. You cannot copy their headcount, their internal bench, or the quiet fact that a pilot in that survey is not the same object as a receptionist trying a new inbox on a Tuesday. Take the sequence. Leave the costume.

<!--cta:inline-->

Stop at the stage you cannot finish. A checker you cannot name means you are not ready to keep the work. We would rather you pause on a named page than push a half-built flow into the week the office manager is already losing to the phones.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a neighborhood dental clinic. This is a walk-through we use when an owner asks what the stages look like on a real week. It is not a result we measured. The owner is the dentist, and she still does the exams. The office manager runs the schedule, the billing questions, and the front desk when someone calls in sick. The front-desk lead answers the phone and sends reminders. A hygienist knows which patients are midway through treatment and which ones simply need a cleaning.

The job is narrow. Patients who are due for a cleaning get a short reminder that sounds like the clinic. The dentist does not want a bot booking anything clinical, and she does not want a guess at a balance. She wants the recall message, and she wants a person to see it before it leaves.

We write the job where the front-desk lead can repeat it. Draft the cleaning reminder from the appointment record. Do not mention treatment. Do not offer a price. A person sends it. If a second job is hiding in that sentence, we start again. A seller will try to widen it in the proposal. The sentence is how we say no.

The data gets scored before anyone connects an account. The appointment book lives in the practice software. A paper list in the manager's drawer names people who asked not to be texted. Insurance notes sit on another screen. The hygienist knows which patients are angry about a bill. Those sources disagree. A draft built only from the appointment book will write to someone on the paper list. That is the clinic telling the truth about its files, and it shows up on the first Monday if anyone looks.

The process is a sequence of hands. Monday morning the front-desk lead pulls the due list. The draft uses the appointment record only. Anything that smells like a treatment word goes to the hygienist. The office manager reads the rest and sends it. If she is out, the queue waits. Nobody sends it because the draft looked sure of itself.

The checker is the office manager, named, with time held on the calendar. If she cannot do it, the hygienist is the named backup. "Whoever is free" is not a checker.

After a run of real Mondays they look at what the manager rejected. Wording problems mean they keep the job and tighten the line. Wrong people mean they stop sending and fix the paper list and the appointment book. Stopping is a finished stage. The demo took an afternoon. The paper list and the rule about waiting took the month.

## How we'd run it

We run the stages in order. We do not open the next one while the current one is still a shrug.

First, we sit with the owner and with one person who does the job by hand. We ask to see last week's work on the screen they actually use. We write one sentence that names the job, the input, and the thing the tool must not touch. If they want several jobs, we pick the one that happens every week and hurts when it is late. The rest stay on a closed list. Opening that list is how a reminder becomes "the whole patient experience" before anyone has sent a real one.

Second, we score the data in the room. Where does the record live, who types it, what happens when it is wrong, and which other list contradicts it. In the clinic that is the appointment book against the do-not-text drawer. On a trades desk it is the job ticket against the text thread where the customer changed the fixture. In a shop it is the register against the note scribbled on the bag. If nobody can point at the source, we stop. We will not agree to clean it later. Later is how bad names get a green check.

Third, we write a short script for a loud morning. Who pulls the list. What the draft may see. Who reads it. What a strange one does. What happens when that person is out. We read it back to the person who will run it and we change it until they say they would follow it when the phones are bad. A script they will not follow is decoration.

Fourth, we name the checker and we hold the time on the calendar before anything is switched on. We also write where a rejection lands. A side chat does not count. If the reject is invisible, the same mistake returns and everyone treats it as new.

Fifth, we keep or stop, using a rule written before the first live send. Keep means the checker can clear the queue in the time we held, and the rejects are about wording. Stop means we unplug the send step and go back to the files. We do not add another job to soften the stop. We do not let a seller rename the sentence as the opening of a platform.

We stay with the owner through this, not only with the person who bought the license. The owner is who a friend will text. Our part is to read the original sentence again.

## Common mistakes

Starting with the tool is the one we see most. A cousin sends a link, and the first hour is logins. The job is still fog. Connecting an account is easy. You cannot quietly undo messages sent to people who asked to be left alone.

The demo is the next trap. The records on screen are clean because someone prepared them. The do-not-text list is missing. So is the Monday when two people are out. Signing while the sample is still up means you bought a performance.

A checker on a slide and not on a calendar will rot the queue. "The office will review" is not a name. We have watched reminders leave because each person assumed another had looked. The patient hears about a cleaning while they are already in the chair. The apology lands on the front desk, who never agreed to catch it.

Widening a quiet job is how a sensible project turns sour. The reminder feels calm, so someone points the same login at billing. A clumsy reminder is an awkward call. A wrong balance is a trust problem. They do not belong together because they share a password.

Copying a big-company rollout flatters the room and starves the desk. Cisco's pacesetters were 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production, and they work in organizations with more than 500 employees. They have people whose job is the process. You have a manager who also covers lunch. Copy the sequence. Do not copy a stack of pilots.

The emotional mistake is refusing to stop. A stop feels like a public failure, so the limp workflow stays alive. A stopped send, with the reason on the same page as the job, means the framework worked. A tab that is always "being tweaked" means it did not.

## What we'd do

We would make the owner pick one job, and we would walk away if they would not. That sounds stern if you wanted a partner who nods. It is how we have seen this work finish. Use is common. Scaling inside one function is rare. No more than 10% scale agents in any one function. The firms in that thin slice finished a process. They did not win a contest for the most logins.

We would not aim a clinic at the Cisco pacesetter share. Near 13% of a sample of 8,000 leaders, in organizations with more than 500 employees, is a different building. The useful part is what they did. They were 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production because the process was written first. A clinic can copy that with a manager and a calendar hold. It cannot copy it by exhausting a part-time desk and calling the exhaustion progress.

We would keep the old reminder running beside the draft until the manager trusts what she reads. Sellers dislike that, because the product looks optional. It is cheaper than a week of apologies. When she trusts it, we turn the old way off in a sentence the staff can hear, so nobody keeps doing both in secret.

If a tool is already on the card statement, do not ask us to make it sound larger than it is. Ask which stage you cannot finish. A fuzzy job goes back to the [readiness framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework). A charming demo and a bad Monday belong with the [stall note](/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall). A habit that is still forming can sit in the [Forming band](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/band/forming) until the checker has a name. That is a respectable place to be.

## AI Readiness Assessment Questionnaire: The Themes

An AI readiness questionnaire should force four themes into the open before anyone names a product. The themes are where the data lives, whether the process is written, who checks the output, and what decision success means. A form that opens with a logo has already skipped the work.

NIST groups the risk work as Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.[^nist] We are not asking a small firm to stand up a risk program with those labels on the door. We are asking the questionnaire to cover the same ground in plain speech. Govern is who is allowed to decide. Map is what the job actually is. Measure is how you would know the output is wrong. Manage is what you do when it is. A questionnaire that cannot find those four ideas, even in simpler words, is a sales form.

The [framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework) is how to score the answers. The [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) is the longer reading. The [growth guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/growth) is what the check does after the score. Themes come first. A band comes after. A tool comes last, and sometimes it does not come at all.

We like a short questionnaire. Length feels thorough and often hides the blank. If an owner can answer a long run of soft questions and still not say where the record lives, the form dodged the only question that mattered. We would rather four blunt questions that can be answered "we do not know."

## What a public checklist does not claim

The AWS checklist for small and midsize businesses, updated in September 2025, walks an owner through readiness questions.[^aws] It does not publish a percentage of businesses that are ready. The OECD SME AI adoption tool, current in 2026, is a self-assessment aid for smaller firms.[^oecd] It is not a national adoption rate.

That absence is the point of this section, so we will not rush past it. Owners arrive having read a headline that sounds like a share of firms. They want their questionnaire to end in the same kind of share, so they can tell a partner they are above it or below it. Neither of those public pages will give you that share. AWS gives you questions and a way to talk about stages of work. The OECD tool gives a smaller firm a self-check. If your questionnaire prints a readiness rate for "businesses like yours" at the bottom, ask who was counted. If the answer is nobody, you are holding a costume.

We still use those pages. We use them as question prompts, not as a league table. The AWS questions are a decent prod for an owner who has only thought about features. The OECD aid is a decent prod for a smaller firm that does not want an account, a stored answer, or a national story. What you leave with is your own answers. What you do not leave with is permission to say a percentage of your industry is ready. We will not write that sentence for you, because the sources will not write it either.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

Ask where the record of truth lives. Ask which step is written and which step is habit. Ask who can reject the output. Ask what you will stop doing if the answer is weak. Those four questions are the questionnaire.

Say them in the language of the job, or they stay abstract. "Where does the record live?" becomes "When a customer calls about the thing we promised, which page does the person on the phone open?" "Which step is habit?" becomes "What do we do when the usual person is out, and is that written anywhere a new hire could find?"
