"Who can reject the output?" becomes "Who is allowed to say this message does not go to the customer?" "What will we stop?" becomes "If this works, which notebook closes?"

A questionnaire that cannot survive that translation is still a theme list. Themes are not a score. They are the questions you refuse to skip. The growth guide is where we send people once a real score exists and the next move is about the business getting better at the job, not about collecting more questions. Do not open that guide to avoid the four questions. Open it after you have answers you can stand behind.

<!--image:3-->

We also want the questionnaire to record disagreement. If the owner and the person who does the job give different answers, the form should show both, not a negotiated average. The average is how a blank becomes a tick. Write "owner says the binder, dispatcher says her head" and leave it ugly. Ugly is honest. A clean tick that required a compromise in the hallway is how you buy a tool for a process that does not exist.

NIST's four words help us check that we did not drift into product trivia. If the questionnaire never asks who decides, it skipped Govern. If it never asks what the job is in steps a stranger could follow, it skipped Map. If it never asks how you would notice a wrong output, it skipped Measure. If it never asks what you will do when the output is wrong, it skipped Manage. You can fail those tests with a very professional-looking form. We have watched it happen. The form had sections and a logo and nowhere to write "we do not know."

## A worked example

Say we are at the desk of a small electrical contractor, late afternoon, phones finally quiet. There is an owner, a dispatcher, and a lead who actually walks the jobs. This is an example we walk through. It is not a firm we audited, and we are not going to pretend we counted their jobs.

The owner was handed a questionnaire by a software seller. It opened with the product name and asked how many users she might want, whether she liked dashboards, and how soon she could start. None of that is a readiness question. We set it aside and ask our four.

Where does the record of truth live for a booked job? The owner says the job system. The dispatcher says he keeps a whiteboard because the system is wrong by the time a customer changes a time. The lead says she trusts the text the dispatcher sends her in the morning, because the whiteboard and the system have both lied. Three answers. The questionnaire does not get to average them. The record of truth is unresolved, and that is the answer we write.

Which step is written, and which step is habit? The written step is the quote. The owner is proud of the quote template, and she should be. The habit is everything after the customer says yes. Who tells the lead the parking note? Who calls the customer when the part slips? Who decides a job is done enough to invoice? The dispatcher says "we just do it." The lead says she calls the owner when she is unsure, which means the owner's phone is the process. A step that lives in a phone is not a written step. We mark it as habit.

Who can reject the output? This is the question that makes the room go quiet, in a good way. If a tool drafted the morning text to the lead, who could say it is wrong and stop it? The dispatcher assumes he would notice. The lead says she would notice on site, which is late. The owner says she would want to approve messages at first, then admits she will not read them once the week gets loud. So nobody currently has a real reject button. The people theme is blank. We do not fill it with optimism.

What will they stop doing if the answer is weak? The owner wants to stop repeating the same parking notes. That is a real stop. The dispatcher wants to stop rebuilding the day from scratch each morning. Also real. The lead wants to stop arriving without the part. If the questionnaire cannot connect a tool to one of those stops, the tool is a hobby. We write the stop next to the blank, so the blank has a cost they can feel.

We do not end this example with a score. Themes are not a score. The [framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework) is where those answers get words like absent or partial. The [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) is where a band gets explained. What this conversation produced is a form with blanks the owner cannot talk her way out of. That is a finished questionnaire. A finished sale would have been a different meeting, and a worse one.

## How we'd run it

First we throw out any question that starts with a product. If the sentence can be answered by a vendor's brochure, it is not on our form. The owner's seller asked about dashboards. Dashboards are a feature. Features are what you discuss after the themes, and only if the themes survived.

Second we ask the four questions in job language, one job only. At this desk the job is a booked call from the yes to the lead packing the van. We do not questionnaire the whole company. A form about "the business" produces slogans. A form about one job produces places, names, and blanks.

Third we ask each person separately before we let them repair each other's answers. The dispatcher will defer to the owner if she is in the room from the start. The lead will go quiet if the form starts to sound like a test of her. We want the first answer, the one they would give a new hire. Then we put the answers side by side and let the conflict stand.

Fourth we map the answers onto Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage without making anyone say those words out loud. Who decides is Govern. The steps of the booked job are Map. How the lead would know the morning text is wrong is Measure. What the dispatcher does when it is wrong is Manage. If one of those is missing, the questionnaire is not done, no matter how many other boxes are ticked.

Fifth we decide whether a score is even useful yet. If the record of truth is still three answers, a band will only decorate the confusion. We stay with the questions. If the four themes have answers we can point at, we move to the check and then to the growth guide, which is about what to do after you know the state. The guide is not a way to skip the form.

We keep the session short enough that the lead is not late to a job and the dispatcher is not dispatching from the hallway. A questionnaire completed by the owner alone on a Sunday night will be complete and fictional. The person who does the step has to be in the room.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is starting with the tool. The seller's form feels efficient because it ends in a quote. Efficiency here is how you skip the record, the habit, and the person who can say no. You will pay for that skip monthly.

Another mistake is treating a public checklist as a readiness rate. The AWS page, updated in September 2025, does not publish a percentage of businesses that are ready. The OECD aid, current in 2026, is not a national adoption rate. If your notes say "we are ahead of most firms," you wrote a sentence your sources refused to write.

A third mistake is smoothing disagreement. When the owner, the dispatcher, and the lead name different records, the honest questionnaire shows the split. A single tick marked "system of record: yes" is a fiction they agreed to so the meeting could end. The meeting ending is not the goal. The blank is the goal.

We also see forms that ask about attitude. "How excited is your team about AI?" is not a theme. Excitement does not locate the record. A skeptical the lead who can reject a bad text is more ready than a cheerful room with no reject button. Ask about permission, not mood.

The last mistake is a questionnaire with no "stop doing" line. If nothing will be stopped, nothing was decided. You gathered opinions. You did not assess the job.

## What we'd do

We would use a one-page form with those four questions and a place to write two names when the answers conflict. Our opinion is that a long assessment questionnaire is often a way to feel serious without naming the whiteboard. The owner does not need more questions. She needs the dispatcher's answer and the lead's answer on the same sheet, in ink, where a dashboard question used to be.

If we were sitting with them next week, we would not bring a tool. We would bring the four questions again and see if the record of truth has become one place. If it has, we would score it. If it has not, we would still not buy. A questionnaire that cannot produce a no is not an assessment. It is a path to a signature.

## AI Readiness Assessment: What It Measures and How to Score

An AI readiness assessment asks whether a business can put a tool to work. Public indexes and checklists answer that question for different audiences, and they are easy to mix up. This note compares them, then states what the [Readiness Check guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/readiness) scores for the firm actually in the room.

We get asked for "our number," as if readiness were a credit score you could borrow from a headline. A figure about senior leaders at large companies does not tell a clinic whether the front desk and the clinician share one record.

## What the public tools measure

Cisco's third annual AI Readiness Index, released 14 October 2025, surveyed 8,000 senior leaders in organizations with more than 500 employees, across 30 markets and 26 industries.[^cisco] Pacesetters stayed near 13% for three years. Those organizations were 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production, and 50% more likely to see measurable value. 83% of respondents plan to deploy AI agents, and nearly 40% expect agents to work alongside employees within a year. That sample is not a small-business survey.

Owners hear the Cisco line on a podcast and want to know if they are behind. Behind what? Behind a company large enough to put a senior leader on a survey. Pacesetters near 13% of that sample, held for three years, is a humility check for big firms. It is a bad mirror for a practice with a front desk and a couple of treatment rooms. The part that still rhymes is the production gap. The organizations that move a pilot into the real work are the ones with a written job. The demo was never the hard part. If you use Cisco at all in a small firm, use it as a warning against mistaking a pilot for a habit, not as a ranking you are supposed to join.

Gartner reported on 26 February 2025 that 63% of respondents do not have, or are unsure they have, the data management practices AI needs.[^gartner] The same note predicts that through 2026 organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. That is the line we underline when someone wants to skip the record and start with a login. The project stops because the data was never ready. There is no mystery ending.

The OECD SME AI adoption tool, part of the 2026 French Group of Seven Presidency work, is a short self-check for smaller firms.[^oecd] It takes about five minutes, stores no data, and keeps answers in the browser. As of May 2026 it is a pilot, with preliminary validation by Group of Seven governments. It does not publish an adoption rate. We like it as questions you can answer without creating an account. We do not like it as a stand-in for a national share, because it refuses to be one. If a tool will not give you a rate, do not invent one after the meeting.

AWS published an AI readiness checklist in September 2025.[^aws] It walks five steps and sorts a business into four stages: Not yet ready, Emerging, Operational, and Scaling. The stages cover data, the use case, the stack, governance, and the metrics you will watch. The page does not cite an adoption percentage. Stages are descriptions you can argue with. A percentage nobody counted is a rumor with a percent sign.

<!--image:2-->

| Tool | Who it describes | What you leave with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cisco AI Readiness Index | Organizations with more than 500 employees | A comparison with pacesetters, not a score for one small firm |
| OECD SME tool | Smaller firms in the Group of Seven pilot | A short self-check that stays in the browser |
| AWS checklist | A small or midsize business working through stages | Five steps and four stage names |
| Readiness Check | The business taking it | Four scores, a band, and three suggestions per section |

The Readiness Check is the one built for the firm in the room. It educates and routes. It does not diagnose. [Christopher Buzny](/about/christopher-buzny) publishes the method on the [studio site](/).

We draw that line on purpose. A diagnosis says what is wrong with you. A route says where to look next. Owners sometimes want the diagnosis because it sounds more serious. Serious is not the same as useful. If we told a clinic it had failed readiness, we would be borrowing a clinical tone for a business conversation. The check describes a state and points at a next page. That is the promise, and we would not widen it.

<!--cta:inline-->

## What each band means

The check scores from 0 to 100. Bands are Early (0–39), Forming (40–59), Ready (60–79), and Running (80–100).[^check]

- Early: The work that matters still lives in people's heads. The first useful move is to write one workflow down and name who owns it.
- Forming: Pieces of the work are written down. A named owner and one system of record are what turn that into something a team can run.
- Ready: The business can put a new system to work. The open question is which workflow to start with, and who owns it day to day.
- Running: A real workflow already uses the tools. The next gain is the job that still waits on one person.

<!--image:3-->

A band is a state, not a grade. The four scores behind it are data, process, people, and the decision. The check takes five to seven minutes, one question per screen, and returns three suggestions for each section.

Each band describes where you are today. Early means the know-how is still in people's heads, so you write one workflow and name the owner before you shop. Forming is partial writing. The missing pieces are a named owner and one system of record, and without those nobody else can run the job when the usual person is out. Ready means a new system can land. The argument left is which workflow goes first, and who lives with it on an ordinary day. Running means a real workflow already uses the tools. The gain left is the job that still waits on one person, the one everyone routes around because it is "easier to ask her."

People treat Running as the compliment and Early as the scolding. We do not. Early is a clear description, and it is often the honest one. A clinic can be excellent at care and Early at the paperwork around recalls. Those are different skills. The band is about whether a tool has anything solid to stand on. It is not a review of the owner's character.

The next note looks at [how surveys count AI in small businesses](/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses), which is a different question from whether one firm is ready. A survey can talk about firms in general. It cannot say your front desk and your clinician agree on the chart note. Do not let the wide question answer the narrow one.

## A worked example

Say we are in a small physiotherapy clinic after the last patient. One person runs the front desk. One clinician sees most of the repeat visits. This is an example we walk through, not a clinic we measured.

The owner has been shown a tool that would draft recall messages and summarize visit notes. She wants to know if the practice is "ready" before she signs. We refuse to start with the tool. We start with the four scores, in words, the way the check will later put them in a band.

Data, for the recall job, is a mess in the ordinary sense. The front desk lead has a list in the booking screen. The clinician keeps a notebook of people he meant to see again. The owner trusts a spreadsheet she built when the booking screen lost a column. Asked which list is true, they look at each other. That is not a failure of care. It is an absent source of truth. We would not call data "in place" while three lists can disagree and nobody is embarrassed.

Process is partial. The happy path is spoken: The clinician finishes, the front desk lead books the next visit, the patient leaves with a card. The exception is not spoken. What if the patient will not book today? What if the clinician wants a recall in six weeks but the front desk lead only sees open slots this month? What if the note is not finished before the patient reaches the desk? The owner says they "work it out." Working it out is Forming at best. It is not a process a tool can follow without inventing the rest.

People are the surprise, same as in most rooms. The front desk lead already pastes awkward wording into a personal chat tool so the recall text sounds less cold. The clinician did not know. The owner did not know. Nobody has said whether those words may go to a patient. The people score is not about enthusiasm. It is about permission.

The decision is a blank. The owner says success would be "fewer no-shows" and then cannot say who would turn the tool off if a message went to the wrong person. Until that sentence exists, we will not talk about agents, pilots, or pacesetters. Cisco's large-firm picture is interesting and irrelevant to whether the front desk lead and the clinician share a list.

If we scored this room in the check's language, we would expect Early or Forming, and we would say so without flinching. The work that matters for this job still lives in heads and side lists. The useful move is to write the recall workflow down and name who owns it. That is the Early sentence, and it fits.

## How we'd run it

First we name the job. One job. At the clinic it is the recall, from the clinician deciding someone should come back to the patient actually having a time. If the owner says "everything," we shrink it until it has a start and a finish.

Second we pull the public tools apart so nobody borrows the wrong population. Cisco describes organizations with more than 500 employees. The OECD tool is a short self-check that stays in the browser and publishes no rate. AWS offers stage names and does not cite an adoption percentage. None of those is a score for this clinic. We say that before anyone feels behind.

Third we score data, process, people, and the decision in words, using absent, partial, in place, or running only if we can point. The front desk lead, the clinician, and the owner each answer. Disagreement is the finding. We write it down instead of averaging it into a mood.

Fourth we take the check if they want the band. Five to seven minutes, one question per screen, three suggestions per section. We read Early, Forming, Ready, or Running as a state. We do not add a pep talk that turns Early into "almost Ready."

Fifth we pick one next page, not five projects. If the record is the blank, we fix the list the front desk lead and the clinician will both believe. If the writing is the blank, we write the exception for the patient who will not book today. The tool demo can wait until that page exists.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is treating Cisco's pacesetters as a small-business grade. Near 13% of a large-firm sample, 4 times as likely to move a pilot into production, is about those firms. Quoting it at a clinic as "only the top shops are ready" invents a ranking the study did not make.

Another mistake is averaging the four scores into a feeling. Data can be absent while people are eager. Eagerness is not a score. The band names a state, and the useful part is the weak state, not the average comfort in the room.

A third mistake is using the OECD tool's silence as a zero. It does not publish an adoption rate. Silence is not a finding that small firms are unready. It is a tool that refused to pretend.

We also watch owners skip from a band to a purchase in the same sitting. Ready still asks which workflow to start with and who owns it day to day. The band did not pick the vendor. You still have to.

## What we'd do

We would score the clinic in front of us and leave Cisco in the footnote where it belongs. Our opinion: a small practice does not need to know whether it is a pacesetter. It needs to know whether the front desk lead's list and the clinician's notebook are the same list. Until they are, a recall tool will write confident messages from a record nobody owns.

If we were the owner, we would spend the next ordinary weeks on one written recall path, including the patient who will not book at the desk, and we would tell the front desk lead to stop sending patient wording from a personal account until the owner has said what may go out. Then we would take the check again and read the band as a state, not as a prize. If it is still Early, we would believe it.

## AI Readiness Checklist Before You Buy a Tool

An AI readiness checklist is the list you finish before you pay for a tool. We use it when an owner has a demo booked and has not yet named the job. The questions fall into four groups: data, process, people, and the decision. A vendor's feature list is not a substitute for those questions.

The [Readiness Check](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check) scores the same four. The [assessment note](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) compares the public tools. The [data note](/blog/ai-ready-data) stays on the first group. If the process score is the weak one, the [process guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-process-low) is the page we hand over.

We think of the checklist as a brake. The tour looks tidy. The real test is the busy afternoon after it, when nobody remembers which screen is the real one. A tick means you can point. A blank means you cannot, and the blank is the useful part.

## Data and process

Can you name the source of truth for the job? Is it current, and can a system read it without someone retyping it? Is the job written down, including the exceptions, and does one person own the handoff?

We ask them out loud, in front of the person who does the work, not only the person who signs the check. The owner answers from memory. The person at the counter answers from last Thursday. When they disagree, the list has already earned its keep.

Every shop we sit in has more than one place a fact can live: the notebook, the spreadsheet the bookkeeper trusts, the supplier portal, the text thread. The record you mean is whichever of those the next person will believe when they conflict. If you cannot name that one, a new tool becomes another place to hunt.

Then ask whether it is current, and whether a system can read it. A source patched by memory is a souvenir. For an open order, current means the status changed when the part arrived, not when someone remembered to call. If someone still has to retype the record, the tool will wait on that person. Retyping is the job you have not replaced.

The process questions sit beside the data questions because a clean record with no written handoff still stalls. We want the happy path and the exceptions. What happens when the part is wrong, when the customer does not answer, or when the usual person is out? If those live as habit, the tool will follow the happy path and invent the rest. One person has to own the handoff on the day that person is not there. "We all own it" is how a handoff disappears.

Gartner reported in February 2025 that 63% of respondents do not have, or are unsure they have, the data management practices AI needs.[^gartner-data] The same note says that through 2026 organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. We read that as permission to treat the data questions as the main event. A large firm and a counter can fail the same way. The record is not ready, and the project dies after the demo fades.

AWS published a checklist in September 2025.[^aws] It walks five steps and sorts a business into four stages: Not yet ready, Emerging, Operational, and Scaling. The page does not cite an adoption percentage. We like that restraint. A stage name is a description you can argue with. If a page will not tell you how many firms it counted, do not borrow its silence and turn it into a rate.

We use those stage names as labels, not as a grade. Not yet ready means the job is still in one person's head. Emerging means some of it is written and a lot of it is habit. Operational means your staff can run the job without a hero. Scaling means you are repeating a pattern, not discovering it. You do not have to adopt the labels. You do have to say which one fits.

<!--image:2-->

The process guide we linked above is what we open when this half of the list is mostly blank. Fix the writing before you fix the software. A short written handoff, with the exceptions on the same page, beats a tool that assumes the handoff already exists.

## People and the decision

Who may use a tool, and who may send its output to a customer? Those are the people questions, and they are where checklists go soft. "Everyone will use it" is not an answer. A name is an answer. A rule about what can leave the building is an answer.

Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index says 75% of knowledge workers use AI at work, and 46% of those users started less than six months earlier.[^microsoft] 78% of AI users bring their own tools. At small and midsize companies that share is 80%. 60% of leaders worry their organization's leadership lacks a plan and vision to implement AI.

In a small company those figures show up as a person. Someone is already pasting notes into a personal account because the official way is slow. They are trying to finish the day. A checklist that never asks who brought a tool in will miss the real system, which is often the one in a coat pocket.

We ask who touches the tool on a normal day, who may send its words to a customer, and who can stop it when it is wrong. If nobody can stop it, you do not have a people plan. You have a hope that errors will be obvious.

The decision questions are separate. What would count as success, who can stop the experiment, and what happens if the tool is wrong? "Sam will keep an eye on it" is a person. "The customer hears from the record, not from memory" is a decision. "If it sends a wrong message, we turn it off the same day" is a decision. Write them on different lines.

<!--cta:inline-->

A tick list does not say which gap is largest. The Readiness Check turns the same four groups into a band. We still want the paper list first, because a band without a conversation is a costume on a number. The list is the conversation. The band is what you get when you want the same questions scored the same way next time.

<!--image:3-->

One more decision question we add when the room is being polite. What will you stop doing if this works? If the answer is nothing, the tool is a hobby. The checklist is allowed to end with a no. A no that names the blank box is a better outcome than a yes that names a logo.

## A worked example

Say we are sitting after close with the owner of a neighborhood hardware shop. There is an owner, a counter lead, and a bookkeeper. This is an example we walk through. It is not a report of a shop we measured.

The owner wants a tool that drafts the message saying a special order is in, and that suggests which supplier to chase. The demo was slick. The checklist is the part where we ignore the demo.

We start with data. The owner says the source of truth is the computer. The counter lead keeps a notebook because the computer is wrong when a quantity changes at the counter. The bookkeeper trusts a spreadsheet she updates from supplier emails, because the other two disagree and she has to pay someone. The box for one source of truth stays blank. Asked which record he would trust if the owner were out, the counter lead says the notebook, then says he would call the bookkeeper. The source of truth is a person. A person can be the bridge. A person cannot be the record a tool reads.

Then the process. A part arrives, someone calls, the customer picks up, the bookkeeper marks it paid. That happy path is easy. A damaged part goes on the back shelf until the counter lead "deals with it." A customer who does not answer gets one more try, then the order sits. None of that is written, and on days the counter lead is at the other site the handoff has no owner. We refuse to count the happy path as the whole process.

Then people. The counter lead already uses a chat tool on his phone to rewrite messages when he is tired of sounding stiff. The owner did not know. We do not scold him. We write the question the checklist was for. Who may send those words to a customer, and who may not?

Then the decision. The owner says success is less chaos. We push once. Success is that a customer hears about an arrival from the record, not from the counter lead's memory, and that the bookkeeper can see the same status the counter lead sees. If a message goes out wrong, the owner can stop the trial herself. She does not wait for a vendor. That line is what lets her buy later without betting the shop on a login.

We leave with blanks on data and process, a surprise on people, and a decision that is finally a sentence. Nobody bought anything. That is the checklist working.

## How we'd run it

We run it as a short working session, not as homework we email into the void.

First we pick one job. Not the whole business. One job with a start and a finish. In the shop, that job is the special order from the promise to the moment the customer has the part or has been told it failed. If you pick every job, you will tick nothing honestly.

Second we put the people who touch that job in the room. The owner alone will describe the job she wishes existed. The counter lead will describe the job that exists. The bookkeeper will describe the job that gets paid. All three answers belong on the sheet.

Third we walk data, then process, then people, then the decision, and we write blanks in ink. We do not shop for tools in the middle. If someone says the new software would handle that, we write "not handled today" and keep going.

Fourth we read the blanks back and name one owner for the next change. If the source of truth is the blank that matters, the bookkeeper and the counter lead agree what they will treat as the record on ordinary days. The owner's job is to back that choice when it is inconvenient.

Fifth we only then look at tools, with the sheet on the table. Any feature that does not touch a ticked box or a named blank is a distraction. If the blanks are still the whole story, we stop. A process blank goes to the process guide. The same four groups go to the check when we want a band instead of ticks.

We book the session after the rush, short enough that the counter lead is not watching the door. A checklist filled by the owner alone at midnight will be full, and it will be wrong.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is ticking the box you hope is true. "We have a process" often means a binder from a quieter year. If the counter lead cannot find the page that covers a damaged part, you do not have a process for the job you are buying for.

Another mistake is letting the vendor's questionnaire replace yours. Their questions ask whether you can be a customer. Yours ask whether the job can survive contact with a tool. Keep yours, even if yours is a notebook page.

A third mistake is calling a shared inbox a system of record. An inbox is a pile that happens to be searchable. It is current only if someone triaged it. The checklist asks whether a system can read the record without a person retyping. A pile fails that test.

We also watch owners score their own confidence and write only the happy path. Confidence is a mood. The checklist is a pointing exercise. The exceptions are the list.

## What we'd do

We would not buy in the meeting where the checklist is first filled in. We would buy later, for one job, after the source of truth has a name and the handoff has a person. Our opinion is blunt. A tool on top of three records will make another record, and you will pay a fee for the privilege of still calling the bookkeeper.

If we were the owner, we would spend the next stretch of ordinary days making the counter lead and the bookkeeper write status in one place, including the damaged-part case, and we would pause the counter lead's phone tool for customer messages until the owner has said what may be sent. That is a smaller project than a new platform. It is the project the checklist was trying to start.

We would treat a full page of ticks with suspicion, and a short page of blanks with respect. The blanks are the work. The tool can wait.

## An AI Readiness Framework an Owner Can Score

An AI readiness framework is a way to score the business before you score a tool. We use it when an owner wants a plan and all anyone has offered is a product tour. The tour can wait. The score is about the work.

NIST groups AI risk work as Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.[^nist] This note uses four groups an owner can see: data, process, people, and the decision. Each group is absent, partial, in place, or running. Those words are anchors. They are not a percentage. If you cannot point at the thing, you do not get the stronger word. We would rather call data absent than call it running because the owner feels modern.

The [readiness guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/readiness) is the matching page. The [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) is the longer note. The [questionnaire](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment-questionnaire) is the question list. The framework is what you do with the answers once they are on paper: you refuse to turn them into a fake share of "readiness" and you give each group a word you can defend.

## What the bands mean

The Readiness Check scores 0 to 39 as Early, 40 to 59 as Forming, 60 to 79 as Ready, and 80 to 100 as Running.[^check] The check educates and routes. It does not certify a business.

Read those bands as widths, not as medals. Early means the work that matters is still in heads. Forming means some of it is written and the owner of it is fuzzy. Ready means you could put a system on the job without inventing the job at the same time. Running means a real workflow already uses the tools, and the leftover pain is the job everyone still asks one person to do. A band without those sentences is just a number. We do not certify anyone with it. Certification is what a buyer wants to wave at a board. A small firm does not have that board, and we will not pretend the check is a seal.

<!--image:2-->

Gartner said in February 2025 that 63% of respondents do not have, or are unsure they have, the data management practices AI needs.[^gartner-data] Through 2026, organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. A framework that scores data as running while the source of truth is a shared inbox is scoring a wish. We keep that sentence on the wall of the conversation. The research is about respondents in Gartner's note, not about your shop, and it still describes the failure we watch: the project looked alive until the record had to carry it.

Cisco's 2025 index surveyed 8,000 senior leaders in organizations with more than 500 employees.[^cisco] Pacesetters stayed near 13%. Those organizations were 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production. That sample is not a small business. The pattern still matters: production follows a written process, not a demo. If you quote the 13% at a bakery and call the baker "not a pacesetter," you have changed the population. The framework is how we stop that slide. We score the bakery's groups in words. We do not import a large-firm league table and staple it to the pass.

<!--cta:inline-->

Score the four groups in words first. Then run the check if you want the band. Words before numbers is the whole method. Absent, partial, in place, running. If you jump to the band, you will negotiate with the number instead of with the inbox. The number is easier to flatter.

<!--image:3-->

Here is how we assign the words, so they do not become moods. Data is absent when nobody can name the record. It is partial when a record exists and people still keep a side copy they trust more. It is in place when one current source is the one a new person would open, and a system could read it without a retype. It is running when that source is already feeding a job you do every week, and someone notices when a field is wrong.

Process is absent when the steps live in one person's head. It is partial when the happy path is written and the exceptions are folklore. It is in place when the exceptions are on the same page and one person owns the handoff, including the day they are out. It is running when everyone follows that page without a meeting to rediscover it.

People is absent when nobody may send output to a customer and nobody has noticed that someone already does. It is partial when use is informal and rejection rights are unclear. It is in place when a named person may use the tool, a named person may send, and a named person may stop it. It is running when that stop has actually been used, not just promised.

The decision is absent when success is "less chaos." It is partial when success is named and nobody can end the trial. It is in place when success, the stopper, and the wrong-output rule are all sentences. It is running when you have already stopped something because the rule said to. A decision that has never survived contact with a bad week is still a draft.

The band sits on top of those words. It does not replace them. Early, Forming, Ready, and Running tell you the shape. The four words tell you where to work. We have watched owners celebrate Ready and ignore a data score that was still partial. The framework exists so that celebration has to walk past the weak group.

## A worked example

Say we are in a small bakery after the morning rush. One person runs the front. Another runs the kitchen and the special-order book. This is an example we walk through. We did not audit their flour, and we will not invent a before-and-after.

The owner wants a tool that answers catering emails and suggests a quote. The demo replied faster than the front lead. The framework is the part where we ignore the speed and score the job.

Data. The special-order book is a paper notebook in the kitchen. The front lead also keeps notes in the front-of-house inbox because customers write to the shop address. The owner has a spreadsheet of prices that is "mostly current." Asked which record a quote must match, they do not agree. Data is absent for the catering job, even though a notebook exists. A notebook nobody treats as final is not a source of truth. Scoring it "in place" because paper is tangible would be the wish Gartner is warning about, the one where the project later gets abandoned because the data was never ready. We say absent.

Process. The happy path is real: inquiry, the kitchen lead checks the book, the owner prices it, the front lead replies. The exception is a customer who changes the headcount the day before, or a date the kitchen lead already half-promised on the phone. That exception is not written. Process is partial. The happy path is not the process. If we scored process as in place, the tool would invent the headcount change and sound sure about it.

People. The front lead already drafts replies in a personal account when she is behind, then pastes them into the inbox. The owner did not know the drafts touched customer words before he saw them. Nobody is named as the person who may send, and nobody is named as the person who may block a send. People is partial, leaning toward absent on the permission that matters. We do not call partial "good enough" just because the front lead is capable. Capable is not the same as authorized.

Decision. The owner says success is more catering without more evenings. That is almost a sentence. He cannot say what would make him turn the tool off, except "if it felt wrong." Felt wrong is not a rule. Decision is partial. We will not average these four words into a cheerful Ready. Absent data plus partial everything else is an Early or Forming shape, and we would rather say that than borrow Cisco's pacesetter story for a bakery that is not in that sample.

What we leave the owner with is four words and one job. Not a percentage. Not a certificate. The next move is to make the notebook or the inbox the single record, write the headcount exception, and name who may send. Then a band means something.

## How we'd run it

First we pick the job the tool is supposed to touch. At the bakery it is the catering reply, from the first email to a price the kitchen can keep. If the owner says the framework should cover the whole shop, we narrow it. A framework about everything scores nothing.

Second we put the front lead and the kitchen lead in the conversation, not only the owner. The owner describes the price list. The front describes the inbox. The kitchen describes the book. The framework is a pointing exercise. People who do not touch the job cannot point.

Third we assign absent, partial, in place, or running to data, then process, then people, then the decision. We say the word out loud and we wait for someone to object. An objection usually means we were about to flatter the group. We downgrade when we cannot point. We do not upgrade because the demo was impressive.

Fourth we only then look at the check, if they want Early, Forming, Ready, or Running as a band from 0 to 100. The band has to be able to live with the four words. If data is absent, we should not be surprised by a low band, and we should not argue the band upward to protect the owner's mood.

Fifth we choose one group to move up a single step. Absent data becomes partial when one record is named, not when a tool arrives. Partial process becomes in place when the headcount exception is written on the same page as the happy path. We do not try to move all four groups in a week of panic. One step, one owner, then we look again.

Sixth we keep Cisco and Gartner in their proper jobs. They explain why data and production matter in the research. They do not score the bakery. If someone in the room quotes a large-firm index as the owner's grade, we put the framework sheet back in the middle of the table.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is using the strong word because it sounds like progress. Calling a shared inbox "running" is the mistake named above, and it is common because the inbox is busy. Busy is not the same as a source a system can read. Busy is a pile with a pulse.

Another mistake is scoring the owner's ambition instead of the job. The owner wants catering to grow. Ambition is not a group in the framework. The groups are data, process, people, and the decision. If those are weak, the ambition is a wish with a login attached.

A third mistake is importing a pacesetter comparison into a small firm. Cisco's 2025 index is senior leaders at organizations with more than 500 employees. Pacesetters near 13%, and 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production, describe that sample. The bakery is not that sample. The pattern we keep is the written process. The ranking we drop.

We also watch people skip the decision group because it feels soft. It is the group that keeps a trial from becoming a subscription you are afraid to cancel. If nobody can stop the experiment, you do not have a framework. You have a purchase.

## What we'd do

We would score in words and stay there until the words stop embarrassing us. Our opinion: the band is a convenience, and the four words are the work. A bakery that can say "data is absent, and the kitchen lead's notebook is what we will make true" is ahead of a bakery that can quote a readiness percentage it did not earn.

If we were the owner, we would not answer another catering email from a side draft until the inbox and the book agree which one wins, and we would write the headcount change on the same card as the quote steps. Then we would take the check. If the band says Early, we would believe it and keep going. The framework did its job when it stopped a fast yes.

## AI-Ready Data: What a Small Business Needs First

AI-ready data for a small business is one current source a system can read, with a person who knows which fields lie. It is not a warehouse, a lake, or a platform with a serious name. If the answer lives only in someone's head, the tool will invent a second version of it, and the second version will sound sure of itself.

Owners get told to "get their data ready" as if that meant consultants and a new place to store everything. For the job in front of you, ready means smaller. One source. Current enough that the person doing the job believes it today. Readable without a retype. And a human who knows which fields are flattering lies. If you cannot point at that source, stop the purchase.

The [low-data guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-data-low) and the [mid-data guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-data-mid) are the matching fixes. The [checklist](/blog/ai-readiness-checklist) asks the same question before a purchase. Low means you cannot yet name a source. Mid means you have something a system should not trust yet. Neither guide is a shopping list.

## What the research counts

Gartner reported in February 2025 that 63% of respondents do not have, or are unsure they have, the data management practices AI needs.[^gartner-data] Through 2026, the same note says, organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects unsupported by AI-ready data. The page's sample size is not cited here, because the article and its structured data do not agree.

We keep that last sentence because it is easy to launder a percentage into a precision it does not have. 63% is what the note reports about respondents. We will not add a sample size the page does not let us stand behind. The useful part is the shape of the failure: firms go ahead without the practices, and unsupported projects get dropped. Through 2026, the note expects organizations to abandon 60% of AI projects unsupported by AI-ready data. A tool can be full of features and still be unsupported if the record under it is a guess.

A later Gartner article, from January 2026, says that by the end of last year at least 50% of generative AI projects were abandoned after proof of concept.[^gartner-fail] The reasons it names are poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs, and unclear business value.

Read those reasons as ways a proof of concept flatters you. The demo works on a clean slice someone prepared. Poor data quality shows up when the real record arrives, with blank fields and two spellings of the same customer. Inadequate risk controls show up when nobody may stop a wrong output. Escalating costs show up when the retype you hoped to delete is still there, plus a fee. Unclear value shows up when you cannot say what you stopped doing. At least 50% abandoned after proof of concept describes projects that got to look successful once. It is a reason to refuse a proof that uses better data than you actually have.

<!--image:2-->

| Where the knowledge lives | What a tool can do with it |
| --- | --- |
| One person's head | Almost nothing repeatable |
| Documents no system can read | A person still has to retype |
| One system with a current record | The job can be tried |

<!--cta:inline-->

Pick one job. Name its source. If you cannot, stop the purchase and fix the source. That is the whole data test.

The table is the test, and owners try to answer it with a tour of their software instead of a location. If the knowledge lives in one person's head, a tool has almost nothing it can repeat. If it lives in documents no system can read, a person still retypes, which means you bought a second job. If it lives in one system with a current record, the job can be tried. Tried is the honest verb. The table does not promise success. It says the attempt is no longer fiction.

We add one column in conversation that the table does not need to print: who knows which fields lie. A current record can still flatter. The phone number is current and the "approved for the extra work" box is wishful. The person who knows that is part of AI-ready data. A warehouse without that person is a larger place to be wrong.

<!--image:3-->

Two phrases we will not use as substitutes for the source. "We have a lot of data" means a pile. Piles are not current on purpose. "We can export it" means a person can make a snapshot that starts going stale while the file downloads. An export is a document. If no system can read the live record, you are in the middle row of the table, and the person who exports is now the process. Fix the source they are exporting from before you call the export a strategy.

## A worked example

Say we are in the office of a small landscaping company on a weekday morning. One person schedules. Another leads a crew. This is an example we walk through. We are not reporting their routes or their revenue. There is no measured before and after. There is a job, and a question about where its record lives.

The job the owner wants a tool to do is the customer update: what the crew did, what is left, and whether the customer owes a decision about extra work. A vendor showed a draft that sounded like the crew lead, only smoother. The owner liked the sound. We asked where the facts in that draft would come from.

The scheduler says the booking tool is the source. It knows the address and the window. The crew lead says the truth is the note she writes in a group text after the crew walks the yard. The owner keeps a spreadsheet of who has approved extras, because he does not trust the booking tool with money questions. Three homes for one update. A draft from the booking tool alone will miss the yard note and may invent the approval. That second version will sound like the crew lead and be wrong in the way that costs trust.

Where the knowledge lives, in the table's words: partly in one person's head, the crew lead's, until she texts; partly in documents the booking tool does not read, the group text and the owner's spreadsheet; not yet in one system with a current record of the whole job. A system could read the address. It could not read "the side bed was wetter than expected, so we stopped and need a yes on the extra drainage" unless someone retypes that into a field. So the middle row is the honest row. A person still has to retype. Buying the draft tool now adds a voice to the retype. It does not remove it.

We ask who knows which fields lie. The crew lead knows the yard. The scheduler knows which customers answer. The owner knows the spreadsheet falls behind whenever he is on a job himself. The record is split across a text, a schedule, and a sheet, and current means something different in each. For the customer update, current has to mean this morning's yard plus whether the extra is approved. They do not have one place that means both.

What we would not do is start a proof of concept on last month's cleanest jobs. If the proof only runs on yards the scheduler already tidied, it is a performance. The test is a messy yard the crew lead has not typed up yet. That is how a flattering demo joins the projects abandoned after proof of concept.

The fix is boring, which is why it works. Pick the customer update as the only job. Pick one place the yard note and the approval must both land before a message goes out. The crew lead's text can stay a scratch pad if the scheduler or the crew lead moves the real sentence into that place the same day. The owner's spreadsheet can stay his private worry list until the approval is also in the shared record. Then a tool can be tried, because there is one current source. Until then, the low-data guide is the right page, not the vendor's order form.

## How we'd run it

First we name the job in one sentence. Not "our data." The customer update, or the open order, or the recall. If the sentence needs a comma splice of every service you sell, we have not named a job. Data readiness without a job is a storage conversation, and storage is how you buy a warehouse you do not need.

Second we ask each person where they would look if the owner were unreachable. The scheduler's answer, the crew lead's answer, and the owner's answer go on one sheet. If the answers match, we still ask whether a system can read that place or whether someone retypes. If the answers do not match, the source is not named, and we stop pretending the booking tool won because it has a logo.

Third we mark the table's row in ink. One person's head, documents no system can read, or one system with a current record. We do not invent a fourth row called "we are getting there." Getting there is the middle row plus a plan. The plan is a person and a place, not a purchase.

Fourth we name who knows which fields lie, and we write the fields. For the crew, the lie is often an approval that was verbal on site and never reached the owner's sheet. That field does not go into a customer message until it is in the shared record. This is the risk-control reason from the later Gartner article, in small clothes: somebody can say the output is not allowed to include a guess.

Fifth we decide low or mid before we decide tool or no tool. If we cannot name the source, we are in the low-data guide and the purchase stops. If we can name it and a person still retypes the part the tool would need, we are in the mid-data guide and the work is to make that part readable. Only the bottom row of the table gets a trial, and the trial has to use the ugly records, not a cleaned sample.

Sixth we reread the research as a brake. 63% without the practices, or unsure they have them. 60% of unsupported projects expected to be abandoned through 2026. At least 50% of generative projects abandoned after proof of concept by the end of last year. Those figures are reasons to refuse a proof that flatters the record. We do not resize them.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is calling an export the source of truth. The scheduler can pull a schedule file any morning. By the time the crew lead is in the yard, the file is a souvenir. The source is whatever will still be right when the customer calls at the end of the day. If that thing is the crew lead's head, say so.

Another mistake is cleaning the data for the demo. Tidy jobs are not the business. A proof of concept that only sees them will pass, then fail when poor data quality shows up. Use a record you are slightly ashamed of.

A third mistake is treating "a lot of history" as readiness. Old invoices in a folder are documents. If no system can read them, a person retypes, and you are in the middle row no matter how many years the folder represents. Volume is not a source.

We also watch owners skip the person who knows which fields lie. The owner knows the approval column goes stale. If he is not in the conversation, the tool will treat that column as fact. The research can talk about data quality. In the room, data quality is a person with a grudge against a specific field. Find that person.

The last mistake is citing a sample size these pages do not give you. The February 2025 page's sample size is not cited here, because the article and its structured data do not agree. Do not fill that gap with a number you heard elsewhere.

## What we'd do

We would not buy the drafting tool for the owner until the yard note and the approval live in one place a message can read. Our opinion is stubborn on this. A smoother voice on a split record is how you send a confident update that the crew lead would not sign. The customer will not blame the data model. They will blame the crew.

If we were the owner, we would pick the update job only, make one shared note the place the crew lead's sentence and the yes on extra work must land the same day, and leave the spreadsheet until it matches that note. Then we would try a tool on a messy yard. If we still cannot name the source, we would stay on the low-data guide and keep the money. One current record is the requirement. A warehouse can wait.

## AI Strategy for Small Business: Start With the Job

An AI strategy for a small business is a short list you can say out loud: the job that changes, the data it needs, and the person who checks the output. It is not a tool catalog, and it is not a slogan about the future. If the page cannot name those three things, you do not have a strategy. You have a pile of apps and a hope that the pile will become a plan by being large.

The [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) scores the same groups of facts we want on that page. The [implementation framework](/blog/ai-implementation-framework) is the sequence after the job is named, when you are ready to do the work in order. The [readiness framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework) is the scoring sheet underneath both. Start with the job. The tools are allowed to wait in the other room, unopened, until the page exists.

We have watched owners skip the page because it felt too small to be serious. Serious, in a company of this size, is one job that survives a busy week. A binder that names every department you do not have is theater.

## Use is ahead of the plan

Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index says 75% of knowledge workers use AI at work.[^microsoft] 46% of those users started less than six months before the survey. 60% of leaders worry their organization's leadership lacks a plan and vision to implement AI. 78% of AI users bring their own tools, and that share is 80% at small and midsize businesses. 55% of leaders are concerned about talent. Only 25% of companies were planning to offer generative AI training. Read that as a picture of a truck cab and a front office that have not met. People are already using the tools. The plan, the training, and the talent worry are behind them.

NIST's risk framework groups the work as Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.[^nist] A strategy that cannot point at those jobs has not started. Govern is who is allowed to decide. Map is where the work and the data actually are. Measure is how you will know the output is wrong. Manage is what you do on the week it is wrong. If your page is only a list of product names, you have skipped all four.

<!--image:2-->

Salesforce surveyed 3,350 leaders at firms of 200 employees and under.[^salesforce] The fieldwork ran through August and September 2024. 75% said they were at least experimenting with AI. Among growing small and midsize businesses, 83% said that. 78% of growing firms planned to increase AI investment, against 55% of firms that were declining. 91% of those already using AI said it boosts revenue. Those are leaders describing their own companies. They are not a promise we will repeat to you as if your revenue had already answered.

<!--cta:inline-->

Those figures describe different populations. Microsoft asked knowledge workers and leaders. Salesforce asked small-business leaders. Neither figure is a substitute for the job you can name on one page. A worker who brings a tool from home, and a leader who says revenue moved, can both be telling the truth about different questions. Your page still has to pick a job.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Walk a heating-and-cooling company that runs a handful of trucks. Example only. Nobody measured this for a report. The owner prices jobs from the driver's seat and has started pasting symptom notes into a personal chatbot. He likes the draft it gives him. He has not told the dispatcher. The dispatcher still builds the board from calls, texts, and a whiteboard that is more accurate than the software they pay for. Two techs trust the board. They do not trust a paragraph the owner forwards at night.

There is no strategy yet, just staff quietly using their own tools. That habit is exactly the pattern in the Microsoft index, where most AI users bring their own tools, and the share is even higher at small and midsize businesses. The owner is not a villain. He found something that unsticks a quote when he is tired. The trouble starts when a customer reads the draft back to the dispatcher the next morning, including a part the shop does not stock and a price the owner would have softened if he had been at a desk.

The office manager finds out in the worst way, which is from the customer. She has no page that says which jobs the tool may touch. She has no rule that a quote leaves only after she or the dispatcher has seen it. She was never trained, because there was nothing to be trained on except "the boss has an app." The Microsoft index saying only a minority of companies were planning generative AI training will feel familiar to her. She is living in the gap between use and a plan.

Here is the page we would write with them, still without a tool name on it. The job is draft estimates for replacement jobs, not for complaints and not for anything that sounds like a safety issue. The data is the price book on the office server, plus the notes the tech already puts on the ticket, and not the owner's memory of a similar house. The checker is the dispatcher, who already knows which crews can do the work this week. If the dispatcher is out, the office manager is the backup, named. If the draft mentions a part they do not stock, it does not leave. That is a strategy. It is short enough to tape inside the cabinet.

Notice what we did not put on the page. We did not put "explore AI across the business." We did not put a chatbot on the website. We did not promise the techs a new identity. The techs need the board to stay right. The owner's night-time draft can survive only if it becomes a draft the dispatcher expects, from sources the office already trusts. Until then, the honest instruction is: stop forwarding the chat to customers.

## How we'd run it

We build the page before we add a login. The order matters more than the stationery.

First, we ask the owner what he already does in private. The chatbot in the truck is the fact. We do not scold it. We write it down as bring-your-own use, which is common, and we separate it from a company plan, which is not. Hiding the habit makes it dangerous. Naming it makes it editable.

Second, we pick one job and write the fence around it. Replacement estimates in. Complaint threads out. Safety calls out. Anything the price book cannot support out. The fence is the strategy. A job without a fence becomes every job by Friday, because the tool will answer any question you type. Willingness is not permission.

Third, we name the data and the checker in the same sitting. For this company the price book and the ticket notes are in, and the owner's unwritten memory is out. The dispatcher checks. The office manager covers. We put a hold on the dispatcher's calendar so "check" is a time and not a virtue. NIST's Map and Measure live here, even if we never say the words in the room. Govern is the owner agreeing the fence is real. Manage is what they do when a draft fails the fence: it does not get forwarded, and the reason gets said out loud once so the techs hear the rule.

Fourth, we train only the people on that page. The dispatcher and the office manager, on this job, with real tickets from last week. We do not schedule an all-hands about the future of the trades. Only 25% of companies in the Microsoft index were planning generative AI training at all. We would rather be inside that planning group for one role than outside it with a motivational meeting. The techs get a simpler lesson: quotes to customers come from the office, not from a forwarded chat.

Fifth, we leave the revenue claim alone. Salesforce heard leaders say use boosts revenue, including a very large share of those already using AI. We will not print that on this company's page as if it were their result. Their result, if they earn one, will be a dispatcher who can clear draft estimates without a surprise part. If they want a score before they start, the [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) and the [readiness framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework) are the sheets. If they want the order of work after the page exists, that is the [implementation framework](/blog/ai-implementation-framework).

## Common mistakes

Writing the strategy as a shopping list is the mistake the vendors hope for. A list of products is not a job, a data source, or a checker. It is a set of invoices. Microsoft's leaders were already worried, at 60%, that leadership lacked a plan and vision to implement AI. A shopping list will not calm that worry. It will add logins.

Pretending bring-your-own use is not happening is the fragile mistake. 78% of AI users bring their own tools, and that share is 80% at small and midsize businesses. Your owner in the truck is normal. If the plan ignores him, he will keep forwarding drafts, and the plan will describe a company that does not exist. Fold the habit in, or forbid it in a sentence he agrees to. Do not do neither.

Training "the staff" in the abstract is how training stays imaginary. The people who need it are the dispatcher and the office manager. A general session lets everyone nod and changes no ticket. The index is blunt that planning for generative AI training was uncommon. Copying that absence is easy. A short session on one job is the repair.

Borrowing another population's revenue line is the flattering mistake. 91% of Salesforce respondents already using AI said it boosts revenue. They were leaders at firms of 200 employees and under, in fieldwork that ran through August and September 2024. They are allowed to say that about themselves. You are not allowed to treat it as your forecast. 75% at least experimenting, and 83% among growing small and midsize businesses, is still a description of leaders, not of your whiteboard.

Skipping Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage because the names sound like a big institution is the last miss. The names are just drawers. Who decides. Where the facts are. How you notice a bad output. What you do next. A heating company can fill those drawers on a single page. If it will not, the strategy has not started, no matter how current the owner's app feels.

## What we'd do

We would tape one page inside the cabinet and we would refuse to start a tool rollout until the page had names on it. That is the opinion we bring into the room. Use is already ahead of the plan. 75% of knowledge workers in the Microsoft index use AI at work, and 46% of those users had started less than six months before they were asked. The plan is the scarce object. Chasing more use, when use is the thing you already have in the truck, is how you stay in the 60% of leaders who worry there is no vision. Make the vision a fence around one job.

We would not tell this owner that AI boosts revenue because 91% of leaders who were already using it said so to Salesforce. We believe leaders answer surveys about their own story. We do not believe that story transfers to a dispatcher who has not seen the draft. 78% of growing firms planned to increase investment, against 55% of firms that were declining. Investment without a checker is how declining firms get a new bill. Spend on the price book, the dispatcher's time, and a rule the techs can repeat.

We would also be plain about talent. 55% of leaders in the Microsoft index are concerned about it, and we share a narrower version of that concern. You probably do not need a new kind of employee. You need the dispatcher to be allowed to reject the owner's draft. That is a talent decision disguised as a software decision. If you cannot give her that permission, do not buy anything. Go back to the [readiness framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework) until the permission exists. Then the [implementation framework](/blog/ai-implementation-framework) can run, and the [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) will have something real to score. A strategy that the dispatcher can spoil is a strategy. A strategy only the owner understands is a hobby with a heading.

## Answer Engine Optimization: What Google Still Requires

Answer engine optimization is the work of being cited when a generative answer is written, and Google still treats that work as ordinary SEO. The new name does not create a new set of rules for your site.

Google's guide says that work is still SEO.[^google] The page has to be indexed, and it has to be eligible for a snippet. Google says it does not use llms.txt, and it says there is no special chunking requirement. No extra schema is required for those features. We translate that for owners as a short list of refusals. You do not get a special file that makes you the answer. You do not get to hide the real page behind a blob of text a person cannot read. You do the unglamorous thing. You publish a page Google can index, a page a snippet can lift, and a page a customer can finish.

The [visibility guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/visibility) is the matching check for whether the site can be cited at all. The [ChatGPT note](/blog/how-to-get-your-business-to-show-up-in-chatgpt) covers crawler files, which are a different switch from this one. The [GEO comparison](/blog/generative-engine-optimization-vs-seo) is the research split, if you want the paper and the click study side by side.

## What the research measured

A 2024 paper on generative engine optimization reports visibility gains of up to 40%.[^geo] Methods that add citations, quotations, and statistics were associated with gains over 40%. On Perplexity the reported gain reached 37%. Position-adjusted word count rose 41%, and a subjective impression score rose 28%. The benchmark used 10,000 queries. Those are research results on pages written to be easier for a generated answer to lift. They are not a promise that your faucet page will move by a set amount because you added a quote.

What we take from the paper, sitting with an owner, is the kind of sentence that got the lift. A citation points at a source. A quotation is someone specific saying a thing you can check. A statistic is a number with a population attached, the way this paragraph is doing. A page that says "we are the best hardware store in town" has none of those. A page that says how a cartridge is measured, quotes the manufacturer's fit note, and tells the reader which handles in the aisle match it, has something an answer can carry. The gain is attached to that kind of writing. It is not attached to the phrase "answer engine" in a footer.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

Pew, in July 2025, found that visits with an AI summary produced a click 8% of the time, against 15% when no summary appeared.[^pew] A citation that nobody clicks is still a citation. Write the page so the click is worth taking.

The drop is the part owners feel in the till, even when they never see the study. If the summary already told the person the cartridge size, they may not need you for the fact. They still need you for the part in stock, the person who will show them the wrench, and the honest line about what you will not do on a Sunday. Put that on the page. The summary can borrow the measurement. The visit is for the counter.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Walk a neighborhood hardware store. This is an example we talk through, not a result. One person works the counter and knows which aisle lies. The question people already ask, out loud and in search, is some version of "can someone cut a key and tell me which cartridge fits this dripping faucet."

The old page says the store sells hardware, paint, and keys, with a phone number and a cheerful sentence about friendly service. It is indexed, barely, and a snippet would have nothing sharp to lift. An answer engine, asked that faucet question, will cite a page that states the measurement, the common mismatch, and what to bring to the counter. The owner's page can be that page. It does not become that page by adding a new acronym to the title.

The counter lead's knowledge is the raw material. He already says, to the person holding a bag of parts, that the stem length matters more than the brand stamped on the handle, and that a photo of the old cartridge saves a second trip. That sentence belongs at the top, in words a summary can quote and a person can use. Under it, the owner writes what the store actually does. Keys cut while you wait on the days the counter lead is in. Cartridges matched if you bring the old one or a clear photo. No plumbing repairs in the wall. The refusal is useful. It keeps the answer honest, and it keeps the click from becoming a disappointed visit.

Roles, not a scoreboard. The owner owns the claims and will not let a page say they repair what they only sell. The counter lead checks the draft against what he says at the counter, because a polished sentence that contradicts him will make the next customer angry. Whoever updates the site, even if that is a nephew, has one job: the page stays indexable, the first sentences answer the question, and the source of any number is visible. If a figure is about their own stock, they say it is theirs. If it comes from a manufacturer sheet, they name the sheet. That is the citations-and-quotations move, done at the size of one shop.

A generated answer might then say the stem length matters and send the person to the owner. Pew's finding is why the page cannot stop at the fact the summary will steal. The summary can explain the stem. The page has to make the trip obviously better. Bring the old cartridge. The counter lead is the one who matches it. The store does not open the wall. Those lines are the reason to click, and they are also the reason the citation does not become a complaint.

## How we'd run it

We would not open with a tool that "does AEO." We would open the page a customer already lands on and ask whether a stranger could act on it.

First, confirm the page is indexed and eligible for a snippet. If it is blocked, thin, or tucked behind a form, stop. Google's guide is blunt that generative features still need an ordinary page. No file substitutes for that.

Second, write the question in the customer's words at the top, then answer it in the next sentences. Key cutting, cartridge match, what to bring. A heading that restates the question helps a person scan, and it gives an answer something clean to lift. This is structure, not a special chunking ritual. Google says there is no special chunking requirement.

Third, add the material the 2024 paper associated with the gains. A real citation, a real quotation, a real figure. For the owner, that might be the manufacturer fit note, a sentence that is actually the counter lead's, and a plain statement of which sizes they stock. Do not invent a study. Do not borrow a number you cannot stand behind if a customer reads it back to you.

Fourth, add the reason to click, knowing a summary may already have stated the fact. Hours in words, what you refuse, who at the counter does the matching, what the person should carry in. Pew's July 2025 read is the context. A click happened 8% of the time when a summary appeared, against 15% when it did not. Write for the person who still has a reason to come.

Fifth, skip the extras Google says it does not need. Do not wait on llms.txt. Do not add schema you cannot explain. Do not rewrite the page as fragments that only a model could love. A person in the aisle is the reader who can hurt you.

Sixth, read the page out loud at the counter. The counter lead corrects anything he would not say. The owner deletes any boast. Then leave it up long enough to see whether the questions at the register start to match the questions on the page. That is the feedback that matters at this size. A visibility score from a vendor is optional. The counter is not.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is treating the new name as a new channel with its own file. Google says this is still SEO, and it says it does not use llms.txt. A shop that spends the week on a special file and leaves the faucet page vague has done the opposite of the guide.

The second mistake is a page that cannot be lifted. No clear answer in the opening lines, no heading a person can scan, a phone number as the only fact. Eligibility for a snippet is a requirement, not a style preference. If a snippet would be empty, an answer will be empty too.

The third mistake is fake precision. The paper's gains, up to 40%, and over 40% where citations, quotations, and statistics were added, describe methods on a benchmark of 10,000 queries. Pasting those percentages into the owner's title would be a lie about her store. Use the method. Do not wear the result.

The fourth mistake is writing only for the summary. You optimize the fact, and you forget the click. When a summary is present, Pew saw a click 8% of the time, against 15% without one. A perfect citation that sends nobody to the counter is a thinner business, even if a dashboard calls it visibility.

The fifth mistake is contradictions between the page and the counter. The page says same-day key cutting. The counter lead is off, and the backup will not touch the machine. The answer cites you, the customer arrives, and you lose the only asset that mattered, which is being believed next time.

The sixth mistake is extra schema as a superstition. The guide says no extra schema is required for these features. Adding markup you do not understand does not repair a page that never answered the question.

## What we'd do

We would rewrite the one page people already need, in the counter lead's words, with the refusal included, and we would ignore the pitch that AEO is a separate craft with a separate invoice. Our opinion is that the paper is useful and the label is not. Visibility gains in a 2024 study are a reason to put citations, quotations, and statistics on the page when you truly have them. They are not a reason to talk differently from the way you talk at the counter.

Google still wants an indexed page a snippet can use. Pew says the click gets rarer when a summary shows up. So the page has to be worth the trip after the answer has already spoken. We would rather the owner be cited for a true sentence about stem length, and then earn the visit, than chase a file Google has said it does not read. If you do one thing after this, open the page that should win the question and see whether a stranger could follow it. That is the work. The acronym can wait in the hallway.

## Business Process Automation With AI: Write the Job

Business process automation with AI starts as a written job. We mean the steps a person already follows, in the order they follow them, with the judgment marked where it actually sits. A model can't follow a job that lives in someone's head. It will invent the missing steps, and the invention will sound sure of itself. Anthropic's December 2024 essay says to start with the simplest solution that works, and to prefer a fixed workflow until the next step actually depends on the last one.[^anthropic] We treat that as operating advice. The tool comes after the page. If the page is blank, the tool is guessing.

If the steps aren't written, stop spending. The [process guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-process-mid) is the matching fix for that blank page. The [automation note](/blog/ai-automation-for-small-business) is which job to pick once you can see more than one. The [agents note](/blog/ai-agents-for-business) is the later question, when a fixed path honestly isn't enough because the next step depends on what the last step found.
