Most rooms we sit in aren't there yet. People are still telling the work from memory, and the telling changes every time we ask.

## The process is the product

The map is the thing you are making. Software is only a way to run that map on a busy Tuesday the same way it ran on a quiet Monday. Microsoft's 2024 index says 75% of knowledge workers use AI, and 46% of those users started less than six months earlier.[^microsoft] Use is already ordinary. A shared plan is not. 60% of leaders worry leadership lacks a plan and vision. 55% of leaders were concerned about talent. Only 25% of companies were planning generative AI training. People are already in the tools. Almost nobody is teaching a shared way to use them.

Staff are already using AI, with or without a plan. 78% of AI users bring their own tools, and 80% do so at small and midsize businesses. At a small firm that usually means a personal login the owner likes and a different tab the office manager likes. The work lands in the shared inbox. The method stays in a browser history. When that person is out, the method is out. That isn't a process. It's a habit with a password. Banning the login without writing the path just moves the habit.

Where the hours sit should decide which job you write first. 60% of time in the work apps was spent in email, chat, and meetings, and 40% in creation apps. Owners often want to automate the part that feels like making something, and they leave the inbox alone. The inbox is the job. The chat thread is the job. The meeting that produces no note is the job. Inside those apps, creation is the smaller share of the time. Automate the daily sorting before you decorate a rare act of writing.

<!--image:2-->

Gartner's January 2026 article says at least 50% of generative AI projects were abandoned after proof of concept by the end of the prior year, citing poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs, and unclear value.[^gartner-fail] We don't read that as a reason to fear the tools. We read it as a description of demos that never had a job attached. Poor data quality shows up when nobody decided which record is the real one. Inadequate risk controls show up when nobody owns the stop. Escalating costs show up when the proof keeps growing because the goal was never a single written path. Unclear value shows up when you can't point at the step that got easier to finish. Then the project gets abandoned, and the writeup blames the model. The missing page never makes the writeup.

<!--cta:inline-->

Write the steps a person already follows. Mark the step that waits for a judgment. Automate the steps that don't. If every step needs a judgment, you don't have a process yet. You have a craft. A craft can still be helped at the edges, with drafts and reminders and a place for the file to land. It shouldn't be sold a machine that pretends to replace the judgment. We'd rather say that on the first call than watch someone fund a pilot that already matches the pile Gartner described.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a trades desk as the example we walk through. This isn't a measured result and it isn't a trophy story. It's the shape of the afternoon we keep seeing when we ask someone to narrate yesterday. The owner prices the work. The office manager answers the phone. A lead tech does the site visit and comes back with a note that is half measurements and half memory. The bookkeeper sends the invoice only after someone says the job is done.

Yesterday's quote starts as a voicemail. The office manager scribbles the name, the street, the room, and a mention of a leak. The lead tech visits, takes photos on a personal phone, and texts a few of them to the owner with a line that says the job isn't bad. The owner opens an old quote, changes a few lines, and sets the price from a similar job they remember. The bookkeeper never sees it until the customer says yes. Sometimes the yes arrives as a text to the owner, who means to forward it and doesn't.

If we sit there and write the path, it becomes ordinary in the best way. The office manager logs the address and the room before the visit is booked. The lead tech files the measurements and the photos before leaving the driveway. The owner prices from that note, and the price is the step that waits. The office manager sends the quote only after the price is on it. The bookkeeper opens the invoice only after the yes is written down. We wouldn't hand the price to a model. The rest is copying, ordering, and waiting for a mark. A simple system can carry the note, nag the tech for a missing measurement, and hold the quote. A person still sends it. What the bookkeeper wants is usually modest: a written yes, a matching price, and the same spelling of the name on the invoice. That's a handoff.

A clinic has the same shape with different nouns. The front desk takes the call. The practitioner decides whether the visit is in scope. Billing waits. Write those steps and the front desk can draft the confirmation while a person still sends it. Skip the writing and someone buys a tool that claims to handle intake, while the practitioner keeps a side pad that becomes the real process. A shop counter looks simpler, which is why owners skip the page. The Saturday clerk and the owner disagree the first time we ask them both how a reorder actually happens. We write both versions down before anyone opens a settings screen.

## How we'd run it

First, we ask the person who did the job yesterday to walk it without improving it. Not the ideal version. The version that happened, including the text and the sticky note. We write their words where they can see them. We don't clean them up yet. Cleaning is how the wish sneaks in.

Second, we ask another person who touches the same job to walk it again. The office manager and the owner almost never tell the same story. Where they disagree, we don't average them into a polite middle. We ask which version the customer actually received. That version wins, because the customer is the only audience that paid.

Third, we write the steps as short sentences a new hire could follow on a tired morning. Each sentence has a person and a thing they produce. The lead tech files the measurements before leaving the driveway. If a sentence has no output, it isn't a step. It's a mood, and moods don't automate.

Fourth, we mark the step that waits for a judgment. On the trades desk that's the price. At the clinic it might be whether the visit is in scope. At the shop it might be whether a regular gets a refund past the posted window. If we can't find the mark, we aren't ready to automate anything, because we don't know what must stay with a person.

Fifth, we automate only the steps that don't wait. Move the note. Remind the person. Hold the draft. File the photo. We use the simplest thing that does that move. A fixed workflow is enough when the next step doesn't depend on a discovery inside the last one. The quote either has a price or it doesn't. That's a gate, not a reasoning problem. We stay with the gate even when a vendor calls it an agent.

Sixth, we run the written path on live jobs while the old path is still allowed, and we watch where people step around it. The workaround is the missing step. We add it to the page and we don't scold the person who stepped around. They're showing us the job we failed to write. We keep a person on the send. The draft can be prepared. The customer-facing word goes out because someone with a name looked at it. Skip that and you have a mailbox that talks.

## Common mistakes

Buying the tool because a neighbor bought the tool is the mistake we see first. The neighbor's job isn't yours, and their judgment may sit somewhere else. We've sat with an owner who purchased a stack of seats, connected nothing to a real quote, and called the quiet that followed a failed pilot. The pilot never had a page. The invoice for the seats still arrived.

Writing the process you wish you had is the next one. The wished-for version has no voicemail and no promise to remember. The real version is made of those. Automate the wish and the staff will keep the real path in a group text while the new system looks empty. Empty gets blamed on adoption. The page described a company that doesn't exist. Write the messy path. Remove one mess at a time after the messy path is visible.

Automating the judgment because it hurts has the best sales pitch. Pricing hurts. Deciding whether a visit is in scope hurts. Telling a customer no hurts. Pain isn't a signal that a model should own the step. Move the chores around it and leave the painful step with a name. If the owner wants that step gone, we ask what they'll do when the model is wrong in front of a customer. A shrug means we don't build it.

Treating personal tools as a moral failure wastes time you don't have. The share of people who bring their own tools is a description, and at small and midsize businesses that share is higher. Ban the personal login without a shared path and people will find another login. Give them the path, then show it on a real job. Training, which few companies were even planning, is how the path survives the first busy stretch.

Calling a proof of concept a strategy is how budgets disappear. A proof of concept is a test of a written step. With no step, you have a demo. When the value stays unclear, the project joins the abandoned pile. Skipping the person who lives in the path is the same mistake in a quieter voice. If the office manager wasn't in the room, the map won't match the phone. If they stumble while reading a sentence aloud, the sentence is wrong.

## What we'd do

We'd refuse the model until the steps fit on one page and a person who does the job has nodded at each line. We hold that opinion when the owner is eager and a vendor is already in the hallway. Eagerness isn't a process. A hallway demo isn't a process. A pile of licenses isn't a process. The page is the process. Everything else is a way to run it.

We'd pick the job that already happens every day in email, chat, or the meeting note, because that's where the hours already are. We'd mark the judgment and keep a named person on it. We'd let a fixed workflow carry the rest. We wouldn't start with an agent or a custom build. If the next step truly depends on what the last step found, we can talk about something smarter, after someone shows us that branch on a real job from last week.

We'd also say the quiet part about training. People are using these tools. Few companies were planning to teach a shared way. A path nobody is shown on a real quote is a folder nobody opens. If you want a test before you spend anything, ask yesterday's doer to write the steps from memory, then ask the person who receives the output what they wish they'd received. If those pages don't match, you've found the work. Name a product after that, not before.

## Generative Engine Optimization vs SEO

Generative engine optimization and SEO are the same craft in Google's guide, and the page still has to be worth reading by a person. The argument that you must pick a side is a sales argument. It is not how the guide is written.

Google says answer-engine optimization and generative-engine optimization are still SEO.[^google] The page must be indexed and eligible for a snippet. Google does not use llms.txt. There is no special chunking requirement. We keep those lines together because owners are being told to fund a second program beside the first. The guide does not describe a second program. It describes the page you already owed the reader, now also being quoted inside an answer.

The [visibility guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/visibility) is the check for whether that page can be found and cited. The [answer-engine note](/blog/answer-engine-optimization) is the tactic list if you want the methods in one place. The [llms.txt note](/blog/what-is-llms-txt) is the file Google says it ignores, which is worth knowing before someone sells it as the difference between the two names.

## What changes, and what does not

The 2024 paper reports visibility gains of up to 40% when the page is written for a generative answer.[^geo] Citations, quotations, and statistics were associated with gains over 40%. Perplexity showed gains up to 37%. Position-adjusted word count rose 41%, and subjective impression rose 28%, on a benchmark of 10,000 queries. What changes, in that study, is how visible a source becomes inside the generated answer when the writing carries evidence. What does not change is the need for a real page, on a real site, that a crawler can index and a person can use.

Hold the two layers apart when a proposal blurs them. SEO, in the sense Google is using, gets the page indexed and eligible to be quoted as a snippet. The generative layer is what happens when an answer borrows from that page. You can fail the first layer and never reach the second. You can succeed at being quoted and still fail the business, if the quote satisfied the reader and the visit never happens. Both failures are about the same URL. They are not two departments.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

Pew found, in July 2025, that a visit with an AI summary was followed by a click 8% of the time, against 15% with no summary.[^pew] SEO still gets the page indexed. The generative layer still has to be worth the click.

That is the practical split we want owners to remember. The index is the price of admission. The click is the part that pays the chair time, the associate, the front desk. A page written only to be summarized will do the first job and skip the second. A page written only as a keyword stub will do neither well, because a summary has nothing solid to lift and a person has nothing solid to trust.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Walk a small dental clinic, as an example, not as a case with a score. The front desk lead already answers the same questions the search box gets. The dentist will not let the website invent clinical promises. The question they care about is the one new patients ask before they call: what happens at a first visit, does it hurt to ask about a cracked tooth, and will you see someone who is nervous.

Their current page is an SEO page in the old, thin sense. City name, "family dentistry," a list of services, a map. It might be indexed. A snippet would be mush. A generated answer, asked about a cracked tooth and a nervous patient, will pass over it for a page that says what the first hour is like, what to bring, and what the clinic will not promise. The owner does not need a second site for "generative" readers. She needs this page to carry both jobs.

What does not change is the floor. The page has to be indexed. It has to be eligible for a snippet. The front desk lead should be able to read the opening lines and say, "Yes, that is what I tell people." The dentist should be able to read the clinical lines and not flinch. If those two cannot sign the page, no engine should be quoting it. Google's refusal of special chunking and of llms.txt belongs here too. Chopping the page into fragments, or adding a side file, does not replace the owner's signature on the sentences.

What changes is the shape of the sentences, and the paper is the reason we say so without turning it into a guarantee. Citations, quotations, and statistics were associated with gains over 40% in that 2024 work, on a benchmark of 10,000 queries. For this clinic the honest version is modest. Quote the after-care instruction you already hand out on paper. Cite the professional guidance you actually follow when you talk about a cracked tooth, instead of a blog that sounds clinical. If you mention a figure, it has to be a figure you can explain to a patient who read it in an answer and walked in holding it. Position-adjusted word count and a subjective impression score moved in the study, 41% and 28%. We do not translate those into a target for the owner. We translate them into "write enough real detail that a reader feels the visit before they book."

The click problem sits on top of that, and Pew is why we will not let the page end at the definition of a cracked tooth. A summary can explain the tooth. The page has to explain the owner's clinic. First visits start with a conversation, not a surprise procedure. Nervous patients can say so when they book, and the front desk lead will leave a longer chair. The clinic does not do every specialty, and it will say which ones it refers. Those lines are useless to a summary that only wanted a definition, and they are the reason a person still taps through. When a summary is on the page, the click showed up 8% of the time in Pew's July 2025 read, against 15% when no summary appeared. Write the lines the summary cannot satisfy.

Roles again, because this is where projects get sloppy. The owner approves what the clinic claims. The front desk lead checks the practical lines against the phone script, including the referral list. The dentist owns anything that could be heard as a diagnosis or a promise of no pain. A freelancer can tidy the headings. A freelancer cannot decide the referral list. If the generative work and the SEO work are billed as two projects, you will get two drafts that disagree, and the patient will meet the disagreement at the desk.

## How we'd run it

We would run one page, once, for both names.

First, pick the question the front desk lead answers every week, and only that question. A first visit. A cracked tooth. What you do with a nervous patient. One page per question. A page that tries to be the whole clinic will be quoted for nothing in particular.

Second, make the SEO floor obvious. Indexed, reachable without a gate, eligible for a snippet, opening lines that answer the question in sentences. If a snippet of those lines would embarrass the dentist, they are the wrong lines. Fix them before you worry about any generative layer.

Third, add evidence the way the 2024 paper describes it, and only evidence you have. A citation you would show a patient. A quotation that is actually yours, or actually the patient's instructions you already print. A statistic you can defend. The study saw gains of up to 40% when pages were written for a generative answer, and gains over 40% tied to citations, quotations, and statistics. Perplexity's reported gains went up to 37%. Use the method on your own material. Do not paste the study's percentages onto the clinic.

Fourth, write the click. Say what the summary will not know. How booking works with the front desk lead. What to bring. What you refuse. Which fear you will take seriously. This is the reply to Pew. Being the source is not the same as being visited.

Fifth, refuse the split invoice. Do not hire one vendor for SEO and another for generative engine work on the same URL unless they edit one document. Two strategies produce two tones, and the answer will quote whichever is cleaner, which may be the one the dentist never saw.

Sixth, read it the way the desk will hear it. The front desk lead reads the practical half aloud. The dentist reads the clinical half. The owner asks, "If this is the only paragraph a summary keeps, is it still true?" If the answer is no, cut until it is. Then publish the one page. The names GEO and SEO can both point at it. They do not each get a website.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is believing the names are rival crafts. Google says they are still SEO. A clinic that pauses ordinary indexing work to "move to GEO" has misunderstood the guide. The page that is not indexed is not going to be the cited source.

The second mistake is the side file. Google does not use llms.txt for this. Buying a file, or a service that starts with the file, while the first-visit page stays vague, spends the week on the part the guide shrugs off.

The third mistake is special structure for its own sake. There is no special chunking requirement. Headings that match real questions help humans and give an answer a clean edge to lift. Headings that exist only as bait, with nothing under them, help no one. We would rather see four plain sections a patient can scan than a pile of fragments.

The fourth mistake is importing the study as a forecast for your city. Up to 40%, over 40% with citations, quotations, and statistics, up to 37% on Perplexity, word count up 41%, impression up 28%, benchmark of 10,000 queries. That is what the paper measured. It is not the owner's pipeline. Quoting it on the homepage would be the wrong kind of statistic.

The fifth mistake is ignoring the click. Pew's 8% with a summary, against 15% without, is the business problem hiding inside the visibility win. If you only chase the citation, you can "win" a mention that replaces the visit. Put the un-summarizable detail on the page. The person, the refusal, the way booking actually feels.

The sixth mistake is two owners for one page. A marketing seat edits for keywords. Another edits for answers. Neither sits with the front desk lead. The patient meets the gap. One page, one checker at the desk, one clinician who can veto a line.

## What we'd do

We would keep a single page and a single editor, and we would fire the framing that GEO replaces SEO. Our opinion is that the guide is right and the category fight is not. Write the page so a person can use it. That is what makes it indexable, snippet-ready, and worth citing. The 2024 paper tells you that evidence on the page is associated with more visibility inside generated answers. Pew tells you the click gets harder once a summary appears. Those two facts pull in the same direction. Be specific enough to be quoted, and specific in a way the quote cannot finish.

We would spend the owner's money on the front desk lead's questions and the dentist's veto, not on a second strategy deck. If a vendor cannot show the same URL doing both jobs, they are selling a conflict Google did not ask for. The page still has to exist for the list of links and for the cited answer. One page. Make it true, then make it useful, then leave it where a crawler and a nervous patient can both find it.

## How Can AI Help a Small Business? What Surveys Count

AI helps a small business by taking a named job a person already does. It does not help by moving you closer to a headline. Two surveys from 2025 count AI in small firms, and they count different work. The U.S. Chamber asked who uses generative AI. Statistics Canada asked who used AI to produce goods or deliver services. A firm can say yes to the first and no to the second, and both answers can be honest. This note keeps those claims apart, then names the jobs owners hand over. The [pressure guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/pressure) is the matching question for one business. [Christopher Buzny](/about/christopher-buzny) writes these notes from the [studio site](/).

We sit with owners who have already been told they are late. The number they heard was usually the larger one. First, we figure out what the number actually measures. Help, for a shop or a clinic or a trades desk, is a draft someone checks, a sort someone trusts, a reminder someone still sends. Help is not a rank on a national chart.

## Generative use is not production use

The Chamber's Empowering Small Business report says 58% of small businesses self-identified that they use generative AI, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023.[^chamber] That question asks about generative AI. It does not ask whether AI produces the goods or the service. Self-identified means the owner said so. It doesn't mean an auditor watched the work. It doesn't mean the tool is in the product. An owner who drafts a customer email and then rewrites half of it can answer yes. We would answer yes with them. That yes is real. It is also a different fact from a system that makes the thing the customer bought.

Statistics Canada, in the Canadian Survey on Business Conditions for the second quarter of 2025, found that 12.2% of businesses used AI to produce goods or deliver services, up from 6.1% in the second quarter of 2024.[^statcan] The release is dated 16 June 2025. Collection ran from 1 April to 5 May 2025. The agency received 21,357 responses, of which 9,103 came from businesses that used AI. Read the response counts as a picture of who was asked, not as a target. A large response still describes the questions that were asked. It doesn't turn the generative question into the production question.

<!--image:2-->

Among businesses that used AI, text analytics accounted for 35.7%, and marketing automation for 23.1%. 40.1% had developed new workflows, and 38.9% had trained staff. Those shares sit inside the group that already uses AI. They are not shares of every firm in the country, and they are not shares of the Chamber's generative question. Text analytics is reading and sorting language. Marketing automation is sending and measuring. A new workflow is a path that wasn't written before. Training is a person who was shown the path. Put that way, the list is practical. It is also modest. None of those four is a claim that the business now runs itself.

<!--cta:inline-->

## Jobs an owner can hand over

The Chamber figure describes a tool someone opens. The StatCan figure describes AI inside the delivery of the product or the service. A small business can do the first for a long time without the second. We think that is a sane order. Open the tool on a job you can check. Let production use be a later question, asked only when the goods or the service actually depend on the system. Most owners we sit with are nowhere near that later question, and they don't need to pretend they are.

The jobs that show up in the StatCan breakdown are the practical list: reading and sorting text, sending and measuring marketing, writing a workflow that did not exist, and training the people who will run it. None of those is a promise that the tool will run the business. Reading text looks like an inbox, a pile of referrals, a supplier sheet. Sending marketing looks like a note to people who already bought, not a brand campaign with a film crew. A new workflow looks like a page the front desk can follow when the owner is in a room with a patient. Training looks like sitting with that person once on a real message, not a slide deck titled for a company with a department you don't have.

The [readiness note](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) asks a different question: whether this firm, not the average firm, has the data, the process, the people, and the decision in place. Average firms are what surveys are for. Your firm is a counter, a desk, a schedule. If the readiness questions fail, the survey percentages will not save the project. If they pass, you still don't need the larger percentage as a goal. You need the job.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a clinic as the walkthrough. The owner saw the Chamber figure and felt late, because friends in a group chat were "already using it." The front desk still types appointment reminders by hand. The practitioner still scribbles the after-visit note. Billing still waits for someone to say the visit happened. Nothing in that room is producing care through a model. The care is the practitioner. The model, if it enters at all, enters as a draft of a reminder or a cleaner version of a note the practitioner will still sign.

Walk the reminder, because it's the job that happens every day and a wrong one is obvious. The front desk has the visit on the book. A draft can say the time, the place, and what to bring. The front desk reads it, because some patients need a phone call and some need a short message, and the draft doesn't know the difference. The practitioner isn't in that decision unless the reminder includes a clinical instruction. If it does, the practitioner reads it. Billing doesn't need to see it. That's three roles and one job. We named the handoff.

A shop down the street is even plainer, which is why the headline feels insulting there. The owner sorts supplier mail and customer questions in the same inbox. Sorting is text work. A system can group the supplier sheets away from the sizing questions. The owner still decides which question gets answered before lunch. The goods on the shelf were not produced by a model. Saying the shop "uses AI" because the inbox got grouped is the Chamber kind of yes. Saying the shop uses AI to produce the goods would be the StatCan question, and the honest answer is no.

A trades desk sits between them. The lead tech's site note is text, and turning it into a description the customer can read is a draft. The owner still sets the price. The service is still the repair. You are near the production question only when delivery of the job actually depends on the system, not because a friend forwarded a chart. Until then, hand over the draft and keep the price.

## How we'd run it

First, write down which survey sentence you heard. If it was about generative use, say so in a full sentence. If it was about producing the goods or the service, say that instead. Owners mix them into "most businesses are already doing this," which is not what either source said. The populations are different, and the Canadian production share is the quieter fact.

Second, name one job on your floor that matches the practical list. Reading and sorting. A message you send more than once. A path that isn't written. A person who hasn't been shown the path. Pick the one that already hurts this week. Don't pick the one that would look impressive in a post.

Third, write the roles the way the clinic reminder was written. Who drafts. Who must read. Who is not involved. If everyone is involved, you don't have a handoff. You have a meeting. Training is showing the person who will actually run it.

Fourth, keep the output in a waiting place until the named person acts. A reminder sits. A sorted inbox sits. A rewritten note sits. The send, the order, the published page: those stay human until you can say what happens when they're wrong. For a clinic, wrong means a patient showed up on the wrong day. For a shop, wrong means a regular got a chilly note. For a trades desk, wrong means a price the owner never set. If you can't say the wrongness, you aren't ready to let the draft travel.

Fifth, only after that job has been dull for a stretch, ask the production question on purpose. Does the good or the service depend on this system, or does a person still make the thing while the system handles words around it? If a person still makes the thing, you are in the generative pattern, and that is a legitimate place to stay. The smaller production share is not a reprimand. It's a count of a harder change.

Sixth, check readiness for this firm, not for the average firm. Data you trust, a process someone can say aloud, a person who will own the check, and a decision about what not to automate. The readiness note is that conversation. The pressure guide asks where the business actually hurts. Neither one is a national percentage.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we correct most often is averaging the two surveys into one mood. The Chamber series shows a rise in owners who say they use generative AI. The Canadian series shows a much smaller share using AI to produce goods or deliver services, and it shows what AI-using firms changed afterward. Those are neighbors, not twins. Quote one and you've told a different story than the speaker told. We've heard pitches that borrow the larger figure and then promise the smaller figure's outcome. That's how a draft tool gets sold as a new way to deliver the service.

The next mistake is treating a self-identified yes as a finished operation.  The owner who tried a chatbot on a Sunday can say they use it. The front desk may never have seen the login. The survey can't see that gap, because it asked the business, not each role. When we sit down we ask the person who does the job, not the person who read the article. If those two answers differ, believe the doer.

Reading the tool shares as a quota is how small firms buy things they won't run. Text analytics and marketing automation are common among the Canadian businesses that already use AI. Common is not mandatory. A clinic with no marketing program doesn't need a marketing project so a share looks familiar. A shop that never publishes a page doesn't need a content stack. The workflow share and the training share interest us more than the tool shares, because they describe work after the tool arrived. A firm that adopted, didn't change the path, and didn't show anyone is the firm we worry about, even if their yes was confident.

Skipping the population is how "9,103" starts to sound like a club you failed to join. That figure is responses from businesses that used AI, inside a larger set of responses, in a survey with a collection window. It isn't the number of businesses that have figured out your counter. Use it to remember the claim is grounded. Don't use it as a mirror.

The last mistake is letting the headline pick the job. The owner wants whatever the article seemed to praise. The floor wants the reminder or the inbox. We follow the floor. The article already gave us clean questions. It doesn't get to staff the front desk.

## What we'd do

We'd tell the owner the larger figure and the smaller figure in the same sitting, with the question attached to each, and we'd refuse to pick a tool until they can say which question they actually care about. Most of the time they care about a job, not about production. That's our opinion, and we think it's the kinder one. Chasing the production share before the reminder is reliable is how you buy a system the practitioner will route around.

We'd hand over reading and sorting first, because the inbox is already there. We'd keep a person on anything a customer could feel. We'd write the workflow only for the job we just named, and we'd train the person who runs it before we trained anyone else. A slide for the whole staff can wait. The front desk cannot.

We wouldn't use either survey as a score for the firm in front of us. Surveys measure everyone. The readiness questions measure you. Write the job the way the customer feels it, name the person who checks it, and ignore every percentage until that sentence exists. The percentages will still be true in the morning. Your counter is the thing that can slip.

## How to Show Up in ChatGPT and AI Overviews

Getting a business into ChatGPT search starts with the crawler that search actually uses, which is a different switch from the training crawler. Block the wrong one, or block all of them, and the rest of the writing never gets a chance.

OpenAI documents separate crawlers.[^openai] OAI-SearchBot fetches pages for search results. Opting that crawler out keeps the pages out of ChatGPT search answers. GPTBot is the training crawler. ChatGPT-User fetches when a person triggers a look-up, and robots.txt may not apply to it. They are not one switch. We say that sentence until the owner can repeat it, because the usual robots file treats "bots" as a single mood. Training, search, and a fetch a person just asked for are three different events. A rule written in a hurry will confuse them, and the confusion is silent. The page simply never shows up, and someone blames the copy.

The [visibility guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/visibility) reads the site the way a practical check should, starting from whether a crawler can see the pages at all. The [answer-engine note](/blog/answer-engine-optimization) and the [generative-engine note](/blog/generative-engine-optimization-vs-seo) stay on the vocabulary around Google's summaries. This note stays on the switches, and on the page those switches are supposed to reveal.

## What Google says to do

Google's guide for generative features says the work is still SEO.[^google] It says answer-engine optimization and generative-engine optimization are still SEO from Google's point of view. It says Google does not use llms.txt. It says there is no special chunking requirement. The page has to be indexed, and it has to be eligible for a snippet. No extra schema is required for those features. If you came here only for ChatGPT, do not skip this. A lot of owners want both surfaces, and the Google half of the job is still an ordinary page. A special file will not replace it on either side.

<!--image:2-->

A page that is blocked, thin, or ineligible for a snippet will not become an overview because a new file was added. Allow the search crawler, keep the page indexable, and write the answer where a person can also read it.

We watch this go wrong in a particular order. First the agency blocks every bot "for safety," including the search crawler, and the owner hears that the site is protected. Then someone adds a new file because a thread said the file is how you show up. The page underneath is still a list of cities and a phone number. Nothing in that sequence produces an answer a homeowner can use. The crawler has to be allowed to fetch. The page has to be indexable. The sentences have to be worth repeating. The file is not the sentence.

<!--cta:inline-->

Pew, in July 2025, found that visits with an AI summary produced a click 8% of the time, against 15% when no summary appeared.[^pew] Showing up is not the same as being clicked. Write the page so the citation is worth the click.

That Pew read is about Google summaries, and we still bring it into this conversation. The habit is the same. A generated answer can satisfy the easy part of the question and leave you unvisited. If you win the mention and lose the call, you have done the visible half of the job. The page has to carry the part a summary cannot finish: who rolls the truck, what you will not touch, how a person actually books.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Walk an electrical contractor with us. This is a scene, not a measured result. An office manager runs the office, the inbox, and the site password. Two techs do the work. The question homeowners ask is whether someone can look at a panel that trips, and whether that someone is licensed, insured, and willing to say when the job is a utility problem instead of a house problem.

Their current site is a header, three service words, and a contact form that sometimes fails on a phone. The office manager once pasted a robots file from a forum because a post said AI companies were copying the web. He did not know he had turned away the crawler that fetches pages for search. The owner then paid for a rewrite that added a file at the root and left the service page as thin as before. They were told this would help them show up. It did not, because the search crawler was still unwelcome, and the page still had nothing a citation could honestly repeat.

Separate the switches the way OpenAI separates them. OAI-SearchBot is the one that has to be allowed if ChatGPT search is supposed to fetch the panel page. Opting that one out keeps the page out of those answers, which is a legitimate choice if the owner does not want to be there, and a mistake if she does. GPTBot is the training crawler, and it is a different decision. The owner can refuse training and still want search. She cannot express that difference with a single "disallow all" line she does not understand. ChatGPT-User is the third case. It fetches because a person asked, and robots.txt may not apply to it. The office manager should know that rule exists so he does not promise the owner that a robots file controls every look-up a user can trigger.

The page itself has to survive being read by a person standing in a dark kitchen. Opening lines answer the panel question. What you do on a trip. What you will not do, including anything on the utility side of the meter. How to reach the office manager, and what to say so the right tech brings the right tester. The techs should recognize the description, because they are the ones who will hear "but your website said" in a hallway. The owner signs the claims about license and insurance. The office manager signs the crawler rules, in writing, with the three bots named in words he can point at.

A generated answer might then mention the firm for a tripping panel in their towns. That mention is not the booking. Pew is the reminder, even though it measured a different summary. When a summary is present, a click is less common. So the paragraph the answer cannot replace is the one about the utility boundary and about calling the office manager with a photo of the panel label. The citation gets them interested. The specific refusal gets them to the phone. A thin page gets them a sentence that could have been any electrician in the county.

## How we'd run it

We would touch the robots file and the service page in the same week, and we would not call a new root file the project.

First, write down the three crawlers in the office manager's notebook, in plain words. OAI-SearchBot fetches pages for search. Leaving it blocked keeps you out of ChatGPT search answers. GPTBot is training. ChatGPT-User fetches when a person triggers a look-up, and a robots file may not govern it. If the office manager cannot say those apart, nobody edits the file yet.

Second, decide the training question on purpose. Some owners want no training crawl. That is allowed, and it is not the same lever as search. Make the search choice second, out loud. If the owner wants to be findable in ChatGPT search, OAI-SearchBot has to be allowed to fetch the pages she hopes will be cited. Write the decision next to the file so the next freelancer does not "clean it up."

Third, look at the Google floor on the same pages. Indexed. Eligible for a snippet. Not blocked, not thin, not hiding the only useful sentence behind a form. Google's guide says the generative features are still SEO, that it does not use llms.txt, and that there is no special chunking requirement. No extra schema is required. A page that fails this floor will not become an overview because a file appeared.

Fourth, rewrite the service page in the voice of the kitchen, not the voice of a keyword list. The panel question, the utility boundary, what to photograph, how booking with the office manager works. A person should be able to read it without feeling marketed to. An answer should be able to lift a sentence without inventing the rest.

Fifth, add the reason to click. Assume the summary stole the easy definition of a tripping breaker. Leave the shop-specific part on the page. Who comes. What you refuse. What a homeowner should have ready. Pew, in July 2025, saw a click 8% of the time when a summary appeared, against 15% when none did. Showing up is the citation. The click is a separate piece of writing.

Sixth, test the boring way. Ask someone who does not work there to find the page from the question, on a phone, and to tell you what they would do next. If they cannot tell you, the citation will not save you. Fix the page. Then leave the crawler rules alone unless the owner changes her mind. Stability in the file matters more than a monthly tweak from whoever last read a thread.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is one switch for every bot. A copied robots file that disallows the world will disallow OAI-SearchBot along with GPTBot. You opted out of search answers and called it privacy. If that was the goal, fine. If the goal was to show up, you closed the door and then paid someone to decorate it.

The second mistake is the magic file. Google says it does not use llms.txt. A blocked, thin, or snippet-ineligible page will not become an overview because a new file was added. We have heard the file sold as the ChatGPT trick too. The trick is the crawler plus a page worth citing. The file is a list, when it is anything.

The third mistake is a page only a model could love. Fragments, repeated town names, no sentence a tech would say in a hallway. There is no special chunking requirement. Headings are for people who scan. If a tech would be ashamed to read the page to a customer, it is the wrong page, however well a crawler can fetch it.

The fourth mistake is confusing a mention with a call. The July 2025 Pew finding, 8% of visits with a summary producing a click against 15% without one, is the warning. Write the line the summary cannot complete. The boundary of the work. The photo to send. The person who answers.

The fifth mistake is claims nobody will back. "Same hour" when the truck is across the county. "We repair utility equipment" when you do not. ChatGPT-User may fetch the page because a person asked, and robots.txt may not apply, so a reckless sentence can travel even when you thought you had a gate. Write only what the owner will say in the driveway.

The sixth mistake is handing the file to someone who cannot name the bots. The office manager owns this, or a person the office manager trusts who will explain the diff in words. An anonymous plugin update that "optimizes robots" is how the search crawler disappears again on a Friday.

## What we'd do

We would allow the search crawler, make a separate and explicit choice about training, and spend the real effort on the panel page a homeowner can use. We would not start with a root file, and we would not let a single disallow line stand in for a decision. Our opinion is that most "show up in ChatGPT" projects are a robots accident plus a thin page, wearing a strategy name.

Google still wants an indexed page a snippet can lift, and it still declines the special file and the special schema. OpenAI still uses different crawlers for search, training, and a person-triggered fetch. Pew still says the click thins out when a summary is already on screen. Those three facts are the whole job. Let the search crawler in if you want to be cited. Write the answer where the office manager, a tech, and the homeowner would all recognize it. Then make the next step obvious enough that a citation has somewhere to go.

## How to Use AI in Your Business: Twelve Jobs

How to use AI in a business is a job list, not a model list. Pick a job you already do, write the steps, and keep a person on the output. The model is the last decision, and for plenty of jobs it is a small one. Statistics Canada's 2025 report asked businesses that already use AI which tools they use and what they changed.[^statcan] Among those businesses, text analytics accounted for 35.7%, and marketing automation for 23.1%. 40.1% had developed new workflows, and 38.9% had trained staff. In the same period, 12.2% of businesses used AI to produce goods or deliver services, up from 6.1% a year earlier. Those are descriptions of what firms reported. They are not a shopping list, and they are not permission to open twelve tools on Monday.

The [help note](/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses) separates that production question from generative-AI use. The [automation note](/blog/ai-automation-for-small-business) is how to pick the first job. The [agents note](/blog/ai-agents-for-business) is when the steps branch and a fixed checklist stops being honest. We'd start with one job from the list below. We'd leave the rest in a stack until that one job has a person on it and a week of real use behind it.

## Twelve jobs you can write down

In each job below, AI does the first pass and a person makes the call:

- Draft the customer reply: a person sends it.
- Summarize the meeting: a person accepts the tasks.
- Turn notes into a quote: a person sets the price.
- Sort the inbox: a person decides what is answered.
- Flag the late invoice: a person decides the chase.
- Describe the product: a person approves the page.
- Group support tickets: a person picks the answer.
- Check the inventory exception: a person orders.
- Rewrite the policy in plain language: a person publishes it.
- Compare two supplier notes: a person chooses.
- Draft the weekly report: a person accepts the numbers.
- Prepare the staff answer: a person trains the staff.

Each line has the same shape. A system prepares. A person decides. If you delete the person, you don't have a job. You have a mailbox that hopes. The reply can be drafted from the thread the customer already wrote. Someone who knows that customer still sends it. The meeting summary can list tasks. Someone who was in the room still accepts them, because a model wasn't there to hear the aside that mattered. The quote can be assembled from notes. The price stays with the owner. We keep repeating that shape because owners keep trying to skip the second half. The second half is the business.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

The survey shares above are about businesses that already use AI, except the 12.2% figure, which is all businesses in that Canadian survey. Do not treat a text-analytics share as a share of every firm. Text analytics at 35.7% means that share of AI-using businesses, not of the shop on the corner and not of your street. Marketing automation at 23.1% is the same kind of share. The workflow figure and the training figure, 40.1% and 38.9%, are also among businesses that already use AI. They tell you what changers changed. They don't tell you that a firm which has never tried this is behind, and they don't tell you which of the twelve jobs to run first. The production figure is the odd one out, and it is the one we don't want blurred into the others. Using a tool to draft a reply is not the same claim as using AI to produce the goods or deliver the service.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a shop we keep using as the walkthrough. Not a case, not a scoreboard. A counter, a back room, and three people. The owner buys and prices. A clerk covers the floor and the inbox. A bookkeeper chases what wasn't paid. Yesterday, in this telling, looks ordinary. A customer emailed about a size. A supplier emailed a new sheet. Two invoices sat past the date the bookkeeper cares about. A meeting with a landlord produced a page of scribbles and no tasks. The product page for a new item is still a placeholder. None of that requires a new company. It requires someone to name which of those is the job for now.

Say they pick the customer reply, because it happens every day and a wrong tone with a regular is expensive in a way no dashboard needs to explain. The clerk drops the thread into a draft. The draft pulls the size the customer already mentioned and the line the owner uses for delays. The clerk reads it, changes one sentence because this customer hates cheerfulness, and sends it. The system didn't know about the cheerfulness. The clerk did. That is the whole design. Sort the inbox in the same pass if you want, but a person still decides what is answered today and what can wait until tomorrow. Flag the late invoice on a list the bookkeeper already trusts. The bookkeeper decides the chase. A stiff note to a good account is a judgment. A reminder to a stranger who is sixty days quiet is closer to a rule, and even then we like a person to glance.

The quote job shows up the day the shop does custom work. Notes from a conversation become a description. The owner sets the price. We've watched owners try to let the draft set the price because the draft sounded confident. Confidence isn't a cost. The supplier comparison is the same trap with a different costume. Two notes, two minimums, two lead times written in different formats. A draft can line them up. The owner chooses. Choosing is the job. Lining up is the chore.

A clinic can run the same list without pretending to be a shop. Summarize the meeting, then the practitioner accepts the tasks. Prepare the staff answer, then a person trains the staff. Rewrite the policy in plain language, then a person publishes it. The publish step matters because a policy that sounds friendly and says the wrong clinical thing is worse than a stiff policy that is right. A trades desk lives in the quote line and the inventory exception. The lead tech's note becomes a description. The owner prices. The exception gets checked. A person orders. We are not saying every firm should run all twelve. We are saying each of the twelve is a job with an edge, and the edge is a person.

## How we'd run it

First, write the twelve down where the owner can see them, in the firm's own words. "Flag the late invoice" might mean "the Tuesday list the bookkeeper already prints." Use their name for it. A job you can't say in their language isn't a job you can hand over.

Second, pick one. Use a boring test. It happens often, the output is easy to check, and a mistake is visible before a customer is hurt. The customer reply and the late-invoice flag usually pass that test. The weekly report often fails it, because a wrong number becomes "the record" if nobody is assigned to accept it. Draft the weekly report, then a person accepts the numbers. If you can't name that person, don't start there.

Third, write the steps of that one job the way it happened yesterday, not the way the software brochure describes it. Who receives the message. Who is allowed to send. What "done" looks like. Where the draft waits. If the draft doesn't wait, you skipped the design.

Fourth, run it on live work with the old way still allowed. The clerk can still type a reply from scratch. You're watching whether the draft is useful enough that they stop wanting to. If they keep typing from scratch, the draft is wrong, or the job was the wrong one. Fix that before you add a second job.

Fifth, name the person who checks, in a sentence another employee could read. "The clerk sends customer replies. The owner sends anything with a price or an apology." That sentence will save you more pain than a new model. Group support tickets the same way: the system groups, a person picks the answer. Describe the product the same way: the system drafts, a person approves the page.

Sixth, only then look at a second job. The survey pattern we trust isn't the tool share. It's the pair of follow-on moves: new workflows, and staff who were actually trained. 40.1% and 38.9% are shares among firms already using AI, and even there they aren't everyone. A second job without a workflow and without a person who knows it is how the first job dies. Leave the stack alone until the first job is dull.

## Common mistakes

Starting from a model list is the mistake the title is about. Someone asks which chatbot to buy before they can say which reply they want drafted. The tools will multiply. The jobs won't get clearer. We've sat at tables where three logins were already paid for and nobody could point at a sent reply that had passed through any of them. The money wasn't large. The confusion was.

Treating the survey as a ranking of your firm is the next one. A text-analytics share among AI users is not a grade. A production share across all businesses is a different question, and it is smaller for a reason. Most of the help available to a small firm is still a draft, a sort, a summary. That's allowed. Calling it "AI in the product" when it isn't will make you chase a build you don't need. The help note walks that distinction. Use it before you scare yourself with the smaller figure or flatter yourself with the larger one.

Skipping the person on the output is the mistake that reaches the customer. A drafted reply that goes out alone will eventually be warm to the wrong person, or sure about a price the owner never set. A weekly report that nobody accepts will be quoted in a meeting as if it were the books. A policy rewritten into plain language and published unread can change what staff think the rule is. The second half of every line in the list is there because we have seen the first half travel alone.

Running all twelve at once is impatience dressed up as ambition. The stack exists so you don't. A shop that tries replies, invoices, inventory, the product page, and the staff answer in the same month will do all of them badly and then conclude the tools don't work. They weren't given a job. They were given a pile. Pick one. Let it become boring. Boring is the success condition.

Forgetting training is how the workflow figure and the real room come apart. A new workflow that lives in the owner's head is the old business with an extra tab. Show the clerk on a real thread. Show the bookkeeper on a real late invoice. If the only person who can run it is the person who set it up, you don't have a job. You have a hobby.

## What we'd do

We'd pick the customer reply or the late invoice and refuse every other job for a while. That's the opinion. Twelve examples are still a list. A list doesn't run the counter. One checked job does. We'd write the steps in the clerk's words, put their name on the send, and sit with them once on real mail before we called it installed.

We wouldn't buy a second tool to celebrate the first week. We wouldn't turn the quote price over to a draft because the sentences looked finished. We wouldn't publish a rewritten policy because it sounded friendly. And we wouldn't read 35.7% as a target for our shop. It's a share of a different population, in a Canadian survey, among firms that already use AI. Useful as a map of what those firms touch. Useless as a quota.

If you do nothing else after reading this, circle one line from the twelve and write the name of the person who finishes it. If you can't circle one, you don't have a use yet. You have curiosity, which is a fine place to start and a bad thing to automate. The production question, the one about goods and services, can wait until a job you already do has a person on the output and a path someone else could follow.

## Is My Business Ready for AI? Signs to Read First

A business is ready for AI when a named job can move to a tool without inventing the process on the way. Ready is not a mood and not a purchase. It is a description of the data, the process, the people, and the decision around that job. If any one of those is still a shrug, the job is not ready.

The [Readiness Check](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check) scores that as four bands. Early is 0–39, Forming is 40–59, Ready is 60–79, and Running is 80–100.[^check] Each sentence on the check describes a state. The check does not diagnose. We like that limit. A diagnosis invites shame. A state invites the next piece of work. Early is allowed to be the true state. Plenty of good businesses are Early on the job they just tried to automate, and they are fine at the rest of the work.

The [Early band](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/band/early) and the [Ready band](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/band/ready) spell those states out. The [assessment note](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) compares the public tools. Read the band pages when you want the sentences. Read this note when you want to know which signs to trust before you let a vendor tell you the signs.

## What a large-firm index is counting

Cisco's 2025 AI Readiness Index surveyed 8,000 senior leaders at organizations with more than 500 employees, across 30 markets and 26 industries.[^cisco] Pacesetters stayed near 13% of that sample. Those organizations were 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production. That sample is not a small-business census. A small firm can be Ready on the check and still look nothing like a pacesetter.

We say the last part slowly, because it is the part owners miss. Ready on our check means the named job can carry a tool. A pacesetter in Cisco's index is a large organization in a sample of senior leaders. Near 13% of that sample is about those organizations. It is not a report card for a shop, a clinic, or a trades desk. If a salesperson says you should buy now to catch up with pacesetters, they have glued a large-firm statistic to a small-firm fear. The 4 times production gap is real inside that sample. It does not mean your service writer is late.

Use the index as a picture of a different size of firm. The useful rhyme is that moving a pilot into production follows a written process. The useless move is to decide you are behind a business that staffs a whole crew for the pilot. You have a bay, a desk, and a person who knows the customers. Readiness is whether that person can hand the job to a tool without the job falling apart.

<!--image:2-->

The OECD SME AI adoption tool, part of 2026 Group of Seven work, is a short self-check for smaller firms.[^oecd] It takes about five minutes, keeps answers in the browser, and does not publish an adoption rate. Use it as a second set of questions, not as a national share. We like a second set because our questions can go stale in our own mouths. Someone else's short self-check, with no stored data and no pretend rate, is a good way to see whether you dodged a theme. It will not tell you that small firms in your country are or are not ready. Anyone who finishes it and announces a countrywide rate has added a sentence the tool refused to say.

<!--cta:inline-->

Four signs the work can move: the source of truth is named, the steps are written, a person owns the output, and someone can stop the experiment. Four signs it cannot: the knowledge is only in one head, the exceptions are unwritten, nobody may send the output to a customer, and success has no definition.

The signs are visible if the person who does the job is in the room. "Named" means you can point at one record and the others lose the argument. "Written" means a new person could follow the exceptions, not only the sunny path. "Owns the output" means a human is accountable for what a customer receives. "Can stop" means someone may halt a bad send without asking the vendor.

The negative signs are the same facts turned around. Knowledge in one head feels like loyalty to a great employee, and it is also a single point of failure. Unwritten exceptions feel like flexibility, and they are where a tool will improvise. Nobody allowed to send feels like caution, until you notice someone is already sending from a personal account. Success with no definition is how a pilot becomes a subscription.

<!--image:3-->

A small firm can show the positive signs on one job and the negative signs on another. That is normal, and it is why "is my business ready?" is the wrong question. The honest question is which job. The check's bands describe the state you are in for the way you answered, not a tattoo on the business. Early and Forming are 0–39 and 40–59. They are descriptions. Ready and Running are 60–79 and 80–100. They are also descriptions. None of them means you have purchased a product, and none of them means you have failed as an owner.

## A worked example

Say we are in an independent auto shop on a slow afternoon. One person writes the service tickets. Another is the lead tech. This is an example we walk through. We are not reporting their revenue, their comeback rate, or any other figure, because we did not measure them and we will not fake it.

The owner asked after a vendor showed a tool that drafts customer updates from the ticket. We split the question. Ready for which job? The job on offer is the status text: diagnosed, the customer hears what is wrong, says yes or no, the lead tech proceeds or does not.

Walk the positive signs. Is the source of truth named? The ticket writer says the shop system. The lead tech says she writes the real finding on the paper that stays on the dash, because the system ticket is what the ticket writer had time to type, and the ticket writer is often still with the previous customer. The owner says she trusts whatever the ticket writer texts her. Three candidates. The source is not named. First negative sign, already. Knowledge of the true finding sits with the lead tech's paper and the lead tech's head. That is the "one head" sign, even though the ticket writer has a system. A system that is not believed is not the source of truth.

Are the steps written? The sunny path is. Car in, inspect, call, approve, repair, car out. The exceptions are not. What if the customer does not answer and the bay is needed? What if the lead tech finds a second problem after the yes? What if the ticket writer is off and the other writer does not know the lead tech's shorthand? Unwritten exceptions. Second negative sign.

Does a person own the output? The vendor's tool would send a text. The ticket writer assumes he would glance at it. The lead tech says she would not see it until the customer called angry. The owner says she wants to approve "the important ones," which means there is no rule. Nobody owns the output in a way that survives a busy morning. Third gap.

Can someone stop the experiment? The owner says she could cancel the subscription. That is a commercial stop, not an operational one. An operational stop is: this text does not go out, today, because it is wrong, and the person who sees that is allowed to halt it without a meeting. They do not have that person. Fourth gap.

So the shop is not ready for this job. That is not an insult. The owner runs a respected bay. The signs say the status text would invent a process the ticket writer, the lead tech, and the owner do not currently share. If we put the same shop on the check, we would not be surprised to land in Early or Forming. We would be surprised, and suspicious, if the answers came back Ready while the dash paper still beats the ticket.

What would ready look like, without pretending we watched it happen? The ticket writer and the lead tech agree the ticket is the record, and the dash paper is a scratch pad that gets typed before anyone is texted. The no-answer case and the second-problem case are written where the other writer can find them. The ticket writer owns the text, the lead tech can reject a finding that is not what she saw, and the owner can halt a wrong text the same day. Success means the customer hears the finding the lead tech actually made. That is Ready in the ordinary sense. It does not look like a pacesetter. It looks like a shop that stopped inventing the process inside the tool.

## How we'd run it

First we refuse the wide question. "Is my business ready?" becomes "is this job ready?" The owner does not get to mean the whole shop. She gets the status text, because that is what the vendor is selling. A yes about a different job is a way of changing the subject.

Second we read the large-firm index for what it counted, then say out loud that the shop is not in that census. The fear of being behind pacesetters does not get a vote.

Third we walk the four positive signs and the four negative signs as pairs. Named source or one head. Written steps or unwritten exceptions. A person who owns the output, or nobody who may send. A stopper, or success with no definition. The ticket writer, the lead tech, and the owner each answer. We write conflicts instead of smoothing them. The lead tech's paper versus the ticket writer's ticket is the conflict that matters.

Fourth we open the band pages if a label will help. Early and Ready are states with sentences, not prizes. If the signs are negative, we expect Early or Forming, and we treat a Ready result as a reason to reread the answers, not as a reason to celebrate. The check does not diagnose. Neither do we.

Fifth we use the OECD self-check as a second pass, about five minutes, answers kept in the browser, no adoption rate to misuse. If it surfaces a theme we skipped, we add the theme. If someone tries to turn it into "small firms are behind," we stop them. The tool did not say that.

Sixth we only talk about the vendor after the signs are honest. If the signs are negative, the meeting ends without a quote. If the signs are positive for this one job, we still name who stops the trial before anyone creates a login. Ready includes the brake.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is hearing "ready" as a personality. The owner is decisive, the lead tech is skilled, the ticket writer is careful. None of that answers the signs. A careful writer with two records is not ready for a tool that needs one. Character is not a band.

Another mistake is using Cisco's 13% as a small-business failure rate. It is the share of pacesetters in a sample of large organizations. Quoting it to scare a shop owner is a category error. The sample is not a census of bays and storefronts. We will not nod along when a pitch does it.

A third mistake is counting a subscription cancel button as the ability to stop. The owner can always call the vendor later. The sign we want is someone on the floor who can block a bad customer message today. Later is how a wrong text sits in a customer's phone all afternoon.

We also see owners collect the positive signs as adjectives and skip the negatives. They can name a system, so they ignore that the lead tech does not believe it. Naming a system you do not trust is the one-head problem in a nicer outfit. Look at the negative list on purpose. It is ruder, and it is clearer.

The last mistake is treating the OECD tool's missing rate as bad news. It does not publish an adoption rate. That is restraint. Do not fill the silence with a guess and then feel behind the guess.

## What we'd do

We would answer the owner with the signs, not with a pep talk. Our opinion: most shops that ask "are we ready?" are asking for permission to buy, and the honest answer is often that one job is Forming and the rest of the question is too big. We would rather shrink the question than inflate the readiness.

If we were the owner, we would make the ticket the only record the lead tech is willing to have texted, write the no-answer case where the other writer can see it, and give the lead tech a plain way to kill a message that does not match her finding. Then we would take the check and read the band as a state. If it says Ready, we would still start with one job and a person who can stop it. If it says Early, we would believe the dash paper over the demo.

## Off-the-Shelf AI or Custom Software

Off-the-shelf AI is the right buy when a product already does the job. Custom software is the right build when the job is specific to how this business works and no product covers it. We start there because owners usually start at the opposite end. They hear that serious firms build, or they hear that nobody should build, and both sermons skip the only question that matters. Does a product already do this, with a person you can name on the output? If yes, buy it. If the job depends on your records, your exceptions, and your checker, the product will not invent those. That is the custom case, and it is rarer than the sales conversation suggests.

The [studio](/) takes the work that products do not cover. The [consultant note](/blog/ai-consultant-for-small-business) is what to ask before either path. The [agency comparison](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) is who you hire once you know you're building, or once you know you shouldn't. We'd rather lose a build than construct a chassis for a job a sealed box already does. The box is not an insult. The box is how a small firm stays a small firm instead of accidentally becoming a software company.

## What the surveys count

The Chamber's 2025 report says 58% of small businesses use generative AI, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023.[^chamber] That is a use claim. It is not a claim that those firms built custom software. Use can be a tab someone opened. Use can be a draft inside a product they already pay for. The rise across those years says owners are trying the tools. It doesn't say they hired anyone to pour a foundation. When a pitch borrows 58% and then offers you a custom build, it has changed the subject. The subject was use. The invoice is for a build. Those are not the same purchase.

<!--image:2-->

Salesforce surveyed 3,350 leaders at firms of 200 employees and under.[^salesforce] 75% were at least experimenting. 83% of growing small and midsize businesses said that. 91% of those already using AI said it boosts revenue. The survey does not say whether the tool was bought or built. Read that last sentence twice before you let a revenue line choose your architecture. "At least experimenting" is a wide door. Growing firms saying the same thing is still a wide door. A revenue boost, among those already using AI, doesn't identify the vendor and doesn't identify a codebase you will have to feed. We've heard the revenue line used as a reason to build. The line doesn't know what was bought.

<!--cta:inline-->

If a bought product covers the job, buy it. If the job depends on your records, your exceptions, and your checker, the product will not invent those. That is the custom case. Records means the files you actually keep, not the files a demo assumed. Exceptions mean the customer you treat differently and the job you refuse. The checker means a named person who can say the output is wrong. Miss any of the three and you don't have a custom case. You have a wish that someone will design your business for you while they design the software.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a shop whose reorder already lives in the register. This is a walkthrough, not a result. The owner gets a flag when a staple item runs low. The Saturday clerk trusts the flag enough to pull a box. The bookkeeper doesn't need a second opinion unless the flag is about a special order. A cousin in another trade told the owner to "build something with AI" because the cousin saw a demo. Building here would mean a second list that drifts from the register, a login the clerk won't open on a busy Saturday, and a custom pile that still doesn't know the staple from the special order any better than the flag does. Buy, or rather keep, the product. Spend the attention on the exception the flag gets wrong, and write down who decides that exception. That's the whole project. It might be a setting. It might be a sentence on the wall. It is not a chassis.

A trades desk is where we stop saying buy so quickly. The quote starts as a voicemail, becomes a site note, picks up photos from the lead tech's phone, and waits for the owner to set a price. The office manager sends it only after the price is there. No product they already pay for holds that stack. The accounting tool holds the invoice after the yes. The inbox holds the chaos before it. A bought "AI assistant" can draft a friendly paragraph and still lose the measurement. Custom, in this room, means a path that keeps the measurement, the photo, and the price-shaped hole together until the owner fills the hole. The price stays a hole on purpose. We will not build a system that invents it. If a vendor says their shelf product already does the whole path, make them do yesterday's quote in front of you. If they can, buy. If they redraw your job until it fits their screens, you're back in the custom case, or you're in the case where you change your job to fit a product. Changing the job is allowed. Pretending you didn't is how the build gets blamed later.

A clinic usually looks like the shop until someone describes intake. Plain reminders are a product. Many booking tools already send them. Don't commission a reminder engine so the waiting room can say you built something. The custom candidate is the weird intake: the practitioner's rules about which visits are in scope, the note billing needs, the patient who must be called rather than messaged. If those rules live only in the practitioner's head, a product will not invent them, and a custom build will only freeze a bad guess. Write the rules first. Then see if a product has a place to put them. Only the leftover is a build. We've watched clinics skip to the leftover and then discover the booking tool had a field for it the whole time. The field isn't glamorous. Glamour is a poor reason to hire a developer.

## How we'd run it

First, write the job as a single sentence with a person on the output. The clerk acts on the reorder flag. The owner sets the price after the note is complete. The front desk sends the reminder after reading it. If the sentence has no person, you don't know what you're buying or building. You're shopping for a vibe.

Second, list the products you already pay for and ask, in writing, whether any of them do that sentence. Ask the person who uses the product, not only the person who receives the invoice. The bookkeeper knows whether late invoices are already flagged. The clerk knows whether the reorder flag is a lie. The front desk knows whether reminders already go out. A consultant is useful here when the owner is too close to the demo to see the product they have.

Third, try the shelf product on yesterday's real job before you talk to a builder. Not a sample record. Yesterday's awkward one. The special order. The quote with the missing measurement. The patient who has to be called. If the product survives the awkward one with a person checking it, stop. You have your answer. Custom work that begins before this trial is how you pay to rediscover a checkbox.

Fourth, if the product fails, write down the exact miss. "It can't hold the site photo with the measurement." "It has no place for the practitioner's scope rule." That sentence is the spec. A builder who won't repeat the sentence back is about to build a different job, one their framework likes. The agency comparison matters only after this sentence exists. Before it, an agency is a guess with a team.

Fifth, name the checker in the thing you buy and in the thing you build. A shelf tool without a person is still a risk. A custom tool without a person is a more expensive risk, because you now own the repairs. The revenue comment in the Salesforce survey is not a substitute for that name. A boost, among people already using AI, doesn't tell you who presses send.

Sixth, decide what you will not maintain. Custom software is a relationship with your own exceptions. If nobody on the desk can describe the exception a year from now, don't encode it. Leave it as a human step. The cheapest system is the one that refuses to swallow a judgment. We like that cheapness. It keeps the owner in the business they meant to run.

## Common mistakes

Hearing "most small businesses use AI" and translating it into "most small businesses built their own" is the mistake the Chamber figure keeps feeding. 58% is use. Use went up from the prior years in that report. Use is a login, a draft, a feature inside something you already rent. We've had to say this in rooms where a relative had already told the owner that renting was naive. Renting a product that does the job is the grown-up move. Building a second version of the register is the naive one, and it wears a very serious face.

Letting the revenue line pick the architecture is the next one. 91% of those already using AI said it boosts revenue. That's a report about users, not a promise about your chassis. It doesn't split bought from built. A shop can see a lift from a better reminder inside a tool they have, and a trades desk can see nothing from a custom portal that the office manager resents. The survey can't see your resentment. You can. 75% at least experimenting, and 83% of growing firms saying that, means a lot of people are trying things. Trying is not a blueprint.

Building the solved job because custom feels like ownership is how small firms acquire a second business they didn't want. Ownership of code you don't have time to feed is a liability that looks like an asset in the proposal. The proposal shows a tidy chassis. The Tuesday after launch shows a clerk who still uses the register, plus a system that pages you when a field is empty. You will maintain both. The cousin who recommended the build will not.

Skipping yesterday's awkward job is how the trial lies. Teams test the happy path. The happy path fits every product.
