Your business is the exception: the refund you allow, the visit you refuse, the price you won't put in an email. If the trial never touches those, you learned nothing. You watched a demo with your logo near it. Demand the awkward one. If a seller won't run it, believe them. They told you the product doesn't cover the job.

Freezing unwritten rules into custom software is the mistake that feels like progress. The practitioner's scope rules aren't on a page. The builder interviews them for an hour and encodes the hour. Next month a case shows up that the hour didn't cover. The software is now confidently wrong, and changing it is a project. A product with a blank field would have been more honest. Write the rule until a new hire could apply it. Then decide if it needs software at all.

## What we'd do

We'd buy first, and we'd be stubborn about it. That's the opinion. The default for a shop, a clinic, and most trades desks is the product that already does the sentence, with a named person on the output. Custom is a leftover, not a personality. We don't think building is a sign of ambition. We think building is what you do when the leftover is real and you can point at it without waving.

We'd make any builder repeat the miss before they estimate. We'd make any shelf vendor survive yesterday's awkward job. We'd keep the price, the clinical scope, and the exception for a regular customer in human hands unless a product has a clear place to hold the rule and a person still checks the result. We wouldn't let 58% or a revenue percentage choose. Those numbers count use and reported boosts. They don't count your records.

If you're staring at a proposal this week, put it down and open the tool you already pay for. Try the job once, on purpose, with the person who will live with the result sitting next to you. If it works, you're done, and done is a good outcome. If it fails, you'll have the sentence the custom work has to honor. Either way you won't have bought a chassis to impress a chart.

## What Is an AI Agent? A Plain Answer for Owners

An AI agent looks at what it just found and chooses a step inside bounds you set. A workflow does the steps in an order you already wrote. We use that split every time an owner asks whether the new line on the invoice is an agent or a form with a louder name.

Anthropic's December 2024 essay draws the line in those terms. A workflow runs large language models and tools on a path the builder defined, and an agent lets the model direct its own process and its own tool use.[^anthropic] The essay also says to start with the simplest solution, and to add complexity only when the simpler system fails. We keep that sentence on the table during these conversations. Most of the businesses we sit with are not stuck because the software is too plain. They are stuck because the work still lives in one person's memory, and a vendor asked a model to invent a process nobody had written down.

If those steps are still in someone's head, the matching check is the [process guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-process-low). The [use-case note](/blog/ai-agents-for-business) lists jobs a system might take. The [comparison note](/blog/ai-agents-vs-agentic-ai) stays on the vocabulary, which is where sales pages get slippery.

## When a workflow is enough

Use a workflow when the steps are known: take the email, extract the fields, write the draft, wait for a person. Use an agent when the next step depends on what the last step found, and you cannot write every branch in advance. If you cannot name the stop condition, you do not have either one yet.

Picture a plumbing desk on a loud Monday. A scheduler runs the book. She gets the name, the address, and whether water is on the floor. She asks which room, and whether anyone shut the main off. Those questions do not change because a model showed up. A workflow can hold them: a form, a text to the on-call tech, a line in the book. The fork comes after intake, and that is the part people try to skip.

A restaurant with water through the ceiling is a different promise from a slow drip under a rental sink. The restaurant needs the owner or the senior tech to say whether someone rolls now. The drip can wait for the afternoon route. Vendors offer an agent for that fork. The model would read the note and pick a tech, a part, and a time. We would let it draft the options. We would not let it text a time until the scheduler or the owner has looked. Known order, workflow. Order that depends on what you just learned, maybe an agent, and still a person who can stop the send.

<!--image:2-->

| Kind of system | Who picks the next step | When it fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One prompt | The person at the keyboard | A single draft or a single answer |
| Workflow | The path you wrote | The steps rarely change |
| Agent | The model, inside bounds you set | The path depends on what it finds |

Read the middle column before you read a product page. One prompt means the person at the keyboard is still choosing. They paste the job notes, ask for a reply, and send it themselves. That can save a tired afternoon. It is not an agent, and it does not need to become one. A workflow means you already know the order, and the software repeats it without getting bored or skipping the address. An agent means the model looks at what it just found and chooses a tool. The calendar, the parts list, the text message. The bounds are yours. You decide which tools exist, what the system is forbidden to send, and who holds the stop.

The right-hand column is the test we use with owners. If the steps rarely change, stop shopping and write the path. If the path depends on what the system finds, you may want an agent, and you still want the bounds on one page a new hire could follow. We have watched shops buy the agent column for work that belongs in the first row. The staff then spends the week correcting a machine that was never supposed to decide.

## What the survey actually counts

Owners hear a loud number and assume the trade has already moved past them. McKinsey's 2025 survey says 88% of respondents report regular AI use in at least one business function, compared with 78% a year earlier.[^mckinsey] That is a wide claim. Regular use can be a person pasting a quote into a chat window on a Thursday. It is a different sentence from "we run an agent."

The agent sentences are smaller, and they are the ones we want in the room. 23% say their organizations are scaling an agentic system somewhere in the enterprise. An additional 39% are experimenting with agents. In any one function, no more than 10% say they are scaling agents. Read that last line slowly. Somewhere in a large company is a different fact from "the scheduling desk has an agent in production." Firms under $100 million in revenue are less often at the scaling stage: 29%, against nearly half of firms over $5 billion.

<!--cta:inline-->

Those are enterprise survey shares. They are not a score for one small business. An agent still needs a written process and a person who can stop it.

We say this out loud because the wide percentage gets used as a shove. A vendor will put the 88% line on a slide and talk as if a shop with a few trucks is late. The survey does not say that. It says use is common, and scaling an agent inside a single function is not. If firms with real operations teams are mostly still experimenting, you are allowed to write your process before you buy a system that chooses its own tools. The survey is a count of what respondents said. It is not a definition of an agent, and it is not a grade for your desk. Wooden bars of different heights do not tell the scheduler what to do with the next call.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Stay with the plumbing desk and give everyone a job. This is a walk-through, not a result we measured. The owner takes the hard calls. A scheduler runs the book. Luis and Priya are on the tools.

A property manager calls about a smell in more than one unit. The scheduler opens the job the way she always has. Name, callback number, address, keys, whether anyone is home. That block is a workflow. It should not depend on a model's mood. The note that comes back is messy. One unit had a dishwasher replaced recently. Another has a tenant who shuts the water off and tells nobody. Another unit is vacant. The next step depends on what the scheduler just heard. Which door gets the first visit. Whether the truck should carry a camera. Whether a vacant unit with a smell is a bigger opening than a clogged trap.

An agent, in the sense of that 2024 essay, could read the note, look at the afternoon routes and the parts list, and propose an order. Vacant unit first, camera on the truck, Luis because he did the camera work last week and Priya is already on a job across town. The proposal is the agent's work. The text to the manager is not, until the scheduler accepts the wording and the time. If the model cannot see the route, it should say so and stop, rather than invent an arrival window. The card by the phone says no time goes out unless a person on the desk has tapped yes.

A workflow ends at the form, which is the right ending for intake and the wrong tool for this fork. You cannot pre-write every branch of a messy multi-unit call. A single prompt would be the scheduler pasting the note into a chat box and asking for a polite reply. Fine on a quiet afternoon. It does not watch the route, and it does not send anything.

The owner does not need a lecture on models. He needs to know which decisions the desk may delegate. The scheduler needs propose and send as different buttons. Luis needs the camera on the truck if the camera was the point. If those people cannot point at the control that stops the system, you do not have an agent yet. You have a chatbot wearing a job title, and the customer will hear its mistakes in your voice.

## How we'd run it

We would not start by picking software. We would sit with the scheduler and write what she already does when the phone is mean.

First, name the job in one sentence a new hire could repeat. "Turn a call into a visit the tech can finish, without promising a time the route cannot keep." If that sentence becomes the whole menu, you have not named the job.

Second, write the steps that do not change. Name, number, address, access, what is happening, who is rolling. Use the scheduler's order, not a template's. This workflow is the floor, even if an agent comes later.

Third, mark the forks. A fork is any moment where the next step depends on what the last step found. Which unit, camera or not, emergency or the afternoon route. If you can write it as a rule, it is still a workflow. "Water through the ceiling, page the owner" does not need a model.

Fourth, choose what the model may touch. We allow a draft, a suggested tech, and a suggested part. We forbid sending, pricing, and any sentence about who pays for damage. If the bound says "use your judgment," you have left a hole, and the model will fill it with something polite.

Fifth, name the stop and the person. The scheduler can stop it. The owner can stop it. A tech can kick back a job that arrived without the part. The system stops when a fact is missing, when the time sits outside the route, or when the caller is angry. Stopping is a success.

Sixth, replay recent jobs with the names covered. The scheduler compares the proposal with what the desk actually did. Hunt the confident wrong time. Fix the bounds before a live customer sees a message. Only then draft against today's calls, with send still in human hands. We would repeat that replay until the refusals look right, rather than turn on an automatic text because a trial is ending.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is a rename. The chat box gets called an agent because the invoice said so. If a person still picks every next step, you have one prompt. That can be the right tool. The rename makes the staff expect judgment the box does not have.

The second mistake is skipping the written path because writing feels slow. Every exception becomes the model's problem, including ones a card by the phone could handle. The staff stops trusting the book. The scheduler goes back to memory, plus a fee.

The third mistake is a missing stop. The model may text, and nobody is named to halt it on a bad afternoon. The bad promise is usually small, a time the tech cannot make, and the customer hears it as the business.

The fourth mistake is treating the survey as a target. 23% scaling an agentic system somewhere in the enterprise is not a quota. 10% inside any one function is not a score you are failing. Chasing those shares buys a tool nobody can supervise.

The fifth mistake is letting the system near money. A price, a waived fee, a line about whether the landlord pays. A draft the owner edits is a different product from a message that already left.

The sixth mistake is a bound written as a mood. "Be helpful" is not a bound. "Do not offer a same-day visit unless the owner has marked the job urgent" is a bound. If the scheduler cannot enforce the sentence, the model will be helpful in the wrong direction.

## What we'd do

We would write the scheduler's path before we paid for anything that chooses its own tools. We would keep one prompt for the messy replies, a workflow for intake, and an agent only on the fork where the next visit depends on what the note contains. We would leave send on a human button longer than a vendor likes. Our opinion is plain. An agent is worth the trouble when the branch is real and a named person owns the stop. It is a poor purchase when the process is still a story the owner tells at the counter.

The 2024 essay says to earn the complexity. The 2025 survey says that even large firms, inside any one function, are mostly not scaling agents. We believe both. Then we go sit with the person who answers the phone, because that person already knows where the path breaks, and the software does not.

## What Is llms.txt, and Who Actually Reads It

llms.txt is a proposed text file at the root of a site that lists the pages you most want a model to read. It is a map. It is not a citation, and it is not a ranking.

Jeremy Howard published the proposal in September 2024, and the page was updated in August 2026.[^llmstxt] The idea is a short list of the pages you want a model to read, written so a person can audit it in one sitting. This site already publishes [its own file](/llms.txt). That is a fact about this site, not a traffic statistic. We publish it because we like a clean list of what we stand behind.

Google's guide says Google does not use llms.txt for generative features in search.[^google] Keep that next to the proposal, or the proposal becomes a rumor. A file Google's generative features do not read cannot be the reason you show up in those features. The page still has to be indexed. The page still has to deserve the quote.

The [missing-file guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/missing-llms-txt) is the check if you want to know whether yours is absent, broken, or pointing at junk. The [answer-engine note](/blog/answer-engine-optimization) is what Google does require, which is ordinary SEO on a real page. The [GEO comparison](/blog/generative-engine-optimization-vs-seo) is the research on visibility and the click, if the file conversation has crowded that out.

## What a crawl of the files found

Ahrefs, in a study published in June 2026, looked at 137,210 domains in its web analytics that had traffic in May 2026.[^ahrefs] 28% published an llms.txt file, about 38,000 valid files. 97% of those files received zero requests in May. 96% of the requests that did arrive were bots. 19.5% of requests came from named AI tools, and 12% from audit or scanner tools. Sit with those shares before you schedule a project around the file. Most copies, in that study, were never asked for. When something did ask, it was usually a bot, and only a smaller slice of those requests were named AI tools.

We do not read this as "never publish one." We read it as "do not expect the file to be a doorway." A list nobody requests cannot fix a homepage that says nothing. A list that scanners request is not the same event as a model citing you in an answer a customer sees. The study is a count of requests against files, in one month, on domains that already had traffic. It is not a verdict on the proposal's taste. It is a verdict on how often the file was fetched.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

Publish the file if you want a clean list of your pages. Do not expect Google to read it. Keep the pages indexed and worth citing either way.

The order of that advice is the order we use in the room. Pages first. Index first. A sentence a stranger can use. Then, if you still want the list, a short file that points at those pages and does not point at drafts, tag dumps, or anything you would be ashamed to have quoted. The file is a courtesy and a control. It is not the work.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Walk an independent bookshop. This is an example, not a study, and it has no score. A manager runs the floor and the website on the same tired afternoons. People ask, online and at the desk, for a book for a grieving friend, for something a nine-year-old will actually finish, and whether tonight's reading is still happening. The site has a homepage, an events page that is sometimes stale, and a staff-picks page that is the best thing they have written all year.

Someone on a forum told the manager that models will not understand the shop without llms.txt. He generated a long file that linked every tag, every old event, and a draft page about a book club that never started. It looked thorough. It was a bad map. A model that actually fetched it would have been pointed at stale nights and a club that does not exist. A model that never fetched it, which is the common case in the Ahrefs count, would have changed nothing, and the manager would have spent the evening on the wrong artifact.

What we would want in the file, if they publish one, is short. The staff-picks page. The page that explains how to order a book they do not have on the shelf. The events page, only if the manager updates it when a reading is canceled. Not the tag archives. Not the draft. The proposal, since September 2024 and as updated in August 2026, is a list of the pages you want read. "Want" is the verb. It is not "everything the CMS can emit."

Roles make the file honest. The owner decides which pages represent the shop. If she would not hand that URL to a regular, it does not go in the list. The manager keeps the events page true, because a file that points at a lie is worse than no file. Whoever fetches or fails to fetch is not their audience. The person who needs a book this afternoon is. The staff-picks page has to stand alone if no model ever requests the map. That is the lesson in the request counts. 97% of the valid files in the study got zero requests in May 2026. A shop that only improved the file, and left the picks page mushy, improved the thing almost nobody asked for.

Google sits to the side of this scene on purpose. The guide says Google does not use llms.txt for generative features in search. The owner can publish a beautiful file and still be absent from those features if the picks page is thin, blocked, or impossible to snippet. The answer-engine work is the page. The file is optional housekeeping. We would tell the manager that directly, before he buys a plugin that regenerates the list every night from every URL it can see.

And the request mix matters when someone waves a log at you. 96% of the requests that did arrive, in that June 2026 study, were bots. 19.5% came from named AI tools. 12% came from audit or scanner tools. A hit in a log is not a customer. It is often a machine checking whether the file exists. Treat a scanner hit as a scanner hit. Do not report it to the owner as demand.

## How we'd run it

We would decide whether the list is worth keeping, and we would write it by hand the first time.

First, choose the pages you hope a stranger finds, with the owner in the room. Staff picks. Ordering a title you do not stock. Tonight's reading, if and only if it stays current. If you cannot name them without opening the CMS and scrolling, you are not ready to publish a map.

Second, make those pages good enough to cite with no file at all. Indexed. Clear opening lines. A sentence the manager would say at the desk. Google does not use the file for its generative features, so this step is the one that can affect that surface. The [answer-engine note](/blog/answer-engine-optimization) is the longer version of what "good enough" means. Do not skip it because a file feels more concrete.

Third, write a short llms.txt that points only at those pages, with a line of plain description a person can check. Link the live URL. If the events page is stale, leave it off until the manager fixes it. A short true list beats a long generated one. This site's own file is that kind of choice. It is not evidence that files bring visits.

Fourth, put the file at the root and then forget the fantasy. Ahrefs looked at 137,210 domains with traffic in May 2026 and found that 28% had a file, about 38,000 valid ones. 97% of those saw zero requests that month. If yours is among the quiet majority, the shop does not get to feel broken. The pages are still the product.

Fifth, if you do watch logs, separate machines from people. 96% of requests in the study were bots. Named AI tools were 19.5% of requests. Audit and scanner tools were 12%. A spike from a scanner is not a crowd of readers. Do not rewrite the shop around it.

Sixth, revisit the list when the shop changes, not on a timer. A new picks page, a retired book club, a reading series that ended. The owner removes the dead link the same week. A file that points at last year's calendar is a confident wrong direction. The August 2026 update of the proposal did not change this duty. The list means what it says, or it should not be up.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is expecting Google to fetch it. The guide says Google does not use llms.txt for generative features in search. Publishing one and waiting for AI Overviews is a plan the guide already declined. Fix the page Google can index.

The second mistake is a generated dump. Every tag, every attachment, every draft. The proposal is a curated list. A dump hides the staff-picks page inside noise, which is the opposite of pointing a model at your best work. It also rots, because nobody will curate a thousand automatic lines. We would rather the manager maintain a list he can read aloud.

The third mistake is treating the Ahrefs shares as a personal failure or a personal trophy. 28% of those 137,210 domains had a file. About 38,000 valid files. 97% with zero requests in May 2026. You are not behind because you lack one, and you are not ahead because you have one that nobody requested. The study describes a crawl of files. It does not describe your customers.

The fourth mistake is reading bot traffic as adoption. 96% of the requests that arrived were bots. 12% were audit or scanner tools. 19.5% were named AI tools. None of those sentences say a reader found the shop. Report them as machine requests, or do not report them.

The fifth mistake is letting the file contradict the floor. The events page says Thursday. The file's blurb says Wednesday, copied from an old night. Whichever surface gets quoted, you look careless. One source of truth, the live page, and the file follows it.

The sixth mistake is doing the file instead of the page, because the file is smaller. A map to a vague homepage is still a vague homepage. The pages have to be worth citing whether or not the file is ever requested. That is the whole practical reading of a study where almost all the valid files sat untouched for the month they measured.

## What we'd do

We would publish a short file only after the pages are true, and we would not tell the owner it will bring her readers. Our opinion is that the proposal is a reasonable courtesy and a bad priority. September 2024 was when the idea was written down. August 2026 is when the page was updated. June 2026 is when a large measurement, 137,210 domains, found that 97% of valid files got zero requests and that 96% of the requests which did show up were bots. Courtesy is allowed to be quiet. Strategy is not allowed to ignore a quiet result.

Google has said it does not use the file. So we would spend the manager's evening on the staff-picks page, the ordering explanation, and an events page that survives a cancellation. Then we would add a list of those URLs if the owner likes being able to see, in one place, what the shop claims. We would keep our own file for that same reason, and we would never wave it as proof of traffic. A file is a pointer. The page is the thing a person came for. If you only have time for one, choose the page, and let the pointer wait until the page would survive being read without it.

## Why AI Pilots Stall After the Demo

An AI pilot stalls when the demo worked and the everyday process never did. The room liked what it saw. Monday did not survive contact with the real files, the real handoff, or a person who can say no. Gartner's January 2026 article says at least 50% of generative AI projects were abandoned after proof of concept, because of poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs, or unclear value.[^gartner-fail] We treat that list as a diagnosis, not as a mood. If one of those four reasons is blank on the page, the pilot is already drifting toward the abandoned pile. It just has not been named yet.

The matching fix on our side is the [decision guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-decision-low). The sequence that should have existed before the demo is the [implementation framework](/blog/ai-implementation-framework). The failure we see first, more than any other, is the one in the [data note](/blog/ai-ready-data). A pilot that cannot point at its source of truth is not "early." It is unfinished, and funding another demo will not finish it.

We have sat through the awkward meeting that follows a charming one. The owner is embarrassed. The staff are tired of sample data. Someone suggests a different vendor, as if the vendor were the missing process. The vendor was never the missing piece. The missing piece was a decision.

## Use is not scaling

McKinsey's 2025 survey says 88% of respondents report regular AI use in at least one function, up from 78% a year earlier.[^mckinsey] About one third of organizations are scaling. 23% are scaling an agentic system somewhere, and 39% are experimenting. No more than 10% are scaling agents in any one function. 29% of firms under $100 million in revenue are at the scaling stage, against nearly half of firms over $5 billion.

That spread is the whole story of a stall, told with a ruler. Use went up. The share of firms that can run the thing inside one function stayed thin. A small firm under that revenue line should not hear the larger-firm comparison as a dare. Nearly half of the much bigger firms are scaling, and they still are not the same animal as a dispatcher and an owner. Your stall is allowed to be about your files. It does not have to be about your size.

<!--image:2-->

Gartner said in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.[^gartner-agentic] Read that as a forecast about projects that never grew a process, not as a curse on the idea of software. Cancellation is what happens when cost, value, or control stays vague past the demo. We would rather you cancel on purpose, this month, than drift into that pile later and call it bad luck.

<!--cta:inline-->

A pilot that cannot name the data, the checker, and the value is already in the abandoned pile. Move it into a written process or stop it. A third option, "let's see how the next demo feels," is how the invoice repeats.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Picture a small electrical contractor. This is a walk-through, not a case we are claiming to have measured. The owner still prices the odd jobs herself. A dispatcher builds the day's runs. Two techs send photos from the site. An office lead turns those photos and the customer's text into a quote, when she can get the owner's attention.

They paid for a pilot that summarized inbound texts into a tidy intake note. In the demo, the seller pasted three clean conversations. The note came back with the address, the symptom, and a suggested next step. Everyone nodded. The owner pictured the office lead going home on time.

Monday looked nothing like the paste. The customer had changed the fixture in a later text, then sent a photo of the old one by mistake, then asked whether the price included the permit. The job history lived in a group thread, not in the software the pilot could see. The price book was a spreadsheet on the owner's laptop, named in a way only she remembered. The office lead could not tell whether the summary was safe to send, because nothing in the note said which messages it had ignored.

The data was poor in a specific way. Not "messy" as a vibe. The source of truth was split, and the pilot pretended it was one record. Risk control was a shrug. Nobody was named to stop a quote that sounded sure and was wrong. Cost started as a small subscription and grew when the seller offered a second workflow "while we are in there." Value had been described as saving the office lead's afternoon. Nobody had written what "saved" would look like on a Thursday when the phones were ugly.

So the pilot stalled in the handoff, which is where stalls live. The demo had no handoff. It ended on the summary. The real work ended when a human had to bet the business's name on that summary. The office lead stopped betting. The tab stayed open. The owner kept paying because canceling felt like admitting the demo had fooled her. It had not fooled her. It had shown her a different company, one with clean threads and a price book the software could read.

## How we'd run it

We do not try to "revive" a stalled pilot with encouragement. We run a short decision, in order, and we let the answer be stop.

First, we write the original promise in one sentence, using the words the owner remembers from the sales meeting. For the contractor, that sentence is something like "the office lead gets a trustworthy intake note from the customer's texts." If the sentence cannot be written, the pilot never had a job. We stop there and we say so. Vague hope is not a project you should keep feeding.

Second, we lay the abandonment reasons on the table as questions, not as blame. Is the data good enough to support the sentence. For this desk, can the note see the whole thread, the right photo, and the price book. Are the risk controls real. Who may send a quote, and who must stop one. Is the cost still the cost you agreed, or has it grown a second workflow. Is the value clear enough that the office lead would notice if it vanished. Gartner's list is poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs, or unclear value. Any blank answer is a reason to pause the spend.

Third, we name a checker before we talk about a better prompt. On this desk the checker is the office lead, with the owner as backup on jobs over a threshold they already use for human quotes. If they cannot name her, the pilot is a toy. We also watch her do one real thread while we sit there. Watching is rude to the seller's narrative and very kind to the business.

Fourth, we choose a written process or a stop, and we do it in the same meeting. A written process means the thread, the photo rule, and the price book are sources the note is allowed to use, and the office lead still sends. A stop means the subscription ends and the sentence goes into a folder until the price book lives somewhere a person besides the owner can find. We do not book a second demo to "see it with cleaner samples." Cleaner samples are how the first meeting lied.

Fifth, we tell the staff the decision in plain language. If we keep it, they hear what changes on Monday. If we stop it, they hear that the stop is the decision, not a failure of the office lead's attitude. People will keep nursing a dead pilot if they think the owner is ashamed. Shame is expensive. A sentence is cheap.

## Common mistakes

Calling the stall a delay is the polite version of a lie. The dispatcher says they are "still rolling it out." Rolling out has a date and a person. A stall has a tab and a feeling. If the office lead has quietly returned to the old thread, you are not delayed. You have already chosen the old way and you are paying twice, once in money and once in pretending.

Blaming the model for a split source of truth wastes the next month. The summary was shaky because the price book was a private file and the photo contradicted the text. A newer model will sound more sure about the same gap. Sureness is not knowledge. We have watched owners swap tools and reproduce the stall with better grammar.

Letting the seller define value is how the cost creeps. "Time back" is not a value until the office lead agrees which hour comes back and what she will do with it. If the answer is "she will finally eat lunch," believe her, and then check whether the note actually returns that lunch. If the note creates a new review chore that eats the same lunch, the value was a slogan.

Skipping risk controls because the job "is just admin" is how a bad quote leaves the building. Admin is your voice to customers. A wrong intake note becomes a wrong visit, a wrong part, and a customer who thinks you do not listen. The control is a named person. It is not a checkbox in the software called "human in the loop" that nobody's loop includes.

Funding a fresh demo to avoid the stop conversation is the expensive mistake. Gartner's June 2025 forecast, that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, is what this habit looks like in bulk. You can be one of the projects that cancels with a reason, or one of the projects that cancels later after a longer invoice. We prefer the shorter invoice.

## What we'd do

We would score the stalled pilot before we let anyone fund another demo. That is a strong opinion and we hold it. A second demo feels hopeful. It is usually a way to avoid telling the seller, and the staff, that the first promise had no data behind it. The [decision guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-decision-low) is the page we open in that meeting. If the score says the business is not ready to decide, we still decide. Not-ready is itself a decision to stop spending.

We would not comfort a small firm with the McKinsey use figure. 88% reporting regular use, up from 78% a year earlier, describes opening a tool. It does not describe a quote the office lead trusts. About one third scaling, 23% scaling an agentic system somewhere, 39% experimenting, and no more than 10% scaling agents in any one function: that is the honest neighborhood. 29% of firms under $100 million in revenue at the scaling stage, against nearly half of firms over $5 billion, tells you the middle is hard even before you are small. Being small is not the stall. A missing checker is the stall.

We would also put the data work first, every time, which is why we keep sending owners to the [data note](/blog/ai-ready-data) before we talk about prompts. And if they want the order of stages after they decide to continue, that order is the [implementation framework](/blog/ai-implementation-framework), not a new pilot with a new logo. Our bet is simple. A stopped pilot with a written reason is a healthier company than a live pilot nobody will sign their name to.
